CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
 
16.0.    Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the Indian Constitution, the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985 was enacted by Parliament to set up Administrative Tribunals for adjudication of disputes and complaints with regard to recruitment and condition of services of persons appointed
to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union and the States.
 
16.1.    Administrative adjudication, which is quasi-judicial in nature, is the main function of Administrative Tribunals.  The basic objective of enacting the Administrative Tribunal Act was:
 
(i)
                  to relieve congestion in the ordinary set of courts; and
(ii)                to provide for speedy disposal of disputes relating to service matters.
 
16.2.    The Central Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 provides that the Tribunals shall not be bound by the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 but shall be guided by the principle of natural justice and subject to the other provisions of Administrative Tribunals Act and
rules made by the Central Government.  The Tribunal shall have power to regulate its own procedure including the fixing of places and times of enquiry.  As a result of the judgement of the Supreme Court in the case of L. Chandra Kumar dated 18 March 1997, the appeals against the orders of an
Administrative Tribunals lie before the Division Bench of the concerned High Court.
 
16.3.    Administrative Tribunals are distinguishable from the ordinary courts with regard to their jurisdiction and procedure.  They are free from the shackles of many of the technicalities of the ordinary courts.  The litigant(s) has to submit an application in paper book form prescribed by rule 4 of
Central Administrative Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1985.  It means that every application should be accompanied by the following:-
 
(i)
                  Certified copy of the order against which the application has been filed;
(ii)                All documents relied upon by the applicants and mentioned in the application;
(iii)               Details of the crossed Demand Draft or crossed Indian Postal Order representing the application fee of Rs. 50/-; and
(iv)              Index of documents.
 
16.3.1  The aggrieved person can appear before the court personally.  Government can also present its case through its departmental officers or legal practitioners.
 
16.4.    At present CAT has 17 regular benches, 15 of which operate at the principal seats of High Courts and the remaining two at Jaipur and Lucknow.  These Benches also hold circuit sittings at other seats of High Courts. 
 
16.5.    The Tribunal consists of a Chairman, Vice-Chairmen and Members.  The Members are drawn from both judicial as well as administrative streams so to give the Tribunal the benefit of expertise both in legal and administrative spheres.  The present sanctioned strength of Chairman, Vice-
Chairmen and Members of the CAT is as below:-

circumstances.  The Supreme Court after hearing the matter, in its order dated 29.3.1994 held that once a consent was given by a State Government empowering the CBI to investigate into an offence, the former could not withdraw the same.
 
17.11.3            The Government has also stated that such withdrawal of consent obstructs the functioning of CBI.  However, in view of the judgement of the Supreme Court on the point the legal position has been clarified and the consent once accorded by the State Government cannot be

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS OF THE MINISTRY
 
Non-Plan outlay/Expenditure
 
The projection under the Minor Heads –Salaries of all Departments and attached bodies under Demand No. 63 is Rs 105.5130 crore in BE (2002-2003) as compared to Rs 102.48 crore in BE (2001-2002).  The provision for non-salary expenditure after excluding expenditure on Salaries comes to
Rs 108.177 crore and Rs 122.13 crore in BE (2002-2003) & BE (2001-2002), respectively. The variation of (-) Rs 13.953 crore between BE (2002-2003) and BE (2001-2002) for non-salary expenditure/projection forms (-) 11 percent which conforms to the guidelines of the Ministry of Finance
enumerated in its OM No.7 (4)/E-Coord/2000 dated 24 September 2000.  But it is not understood, from the variation of total Non-plan outlay between BE  (2001-2002) & BE (2002-2003), whether the Ministry has followed the guidelines of the M/o Finance while projecting BE (2002-2003)
under Non-plan outlay.  The 0.5 percent (i.e. Rs. 92 lakh only) reduction under Non-plan outlay of BE (2002-2003) is far behind the goal set by the M/o Finance. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions should strive to take austerity
measures to project more reduction at RE stage (2002-2003) to give effect to guidelines of the Ministry of Finance.
(para 10.8.5)
Plan outlay/Expenditure
 
The Committee is happy to note the objective behind the Centre for Public Policy and urges upon the Ministry to make the training programme fully operational from the current financial year.
(para 10.8.11)
 
The Committee wanted to know the required timeframe within which the modernization of Government Offices was to be completed. The Ministry in its reply has mentioned that modernization of Government Offices is an on-going process. It is not feasible to fix specific time frame for its
completion.  The Committee is not happy with the reply and recommends that the process of modernization which has been going on for the last one decade must be completed within a given timeframe.
(para 10.8.17.)
 
CITIZEN’S CHARTER
 
On examination of the steps taken by those States/UTs, the Committee notes that certain measures taken by them to popularise Citizen’s Charter such as seminars, regular inspections by an appointed official for the purpose, ‘Reader Forum’ incorporated in the Secretariat newsletter, panel
discussion with members of consumer fora, workshops and constitution of Administrative Reforms Advisory Committees are commendable and desires that these may be used as guidelines for the States/UTs who have not furnished the steps taken by them to the Ministry. The Committee, while
reiterating its earlier view that publicity of Citizens’ Charters is very essential to make the general public aware about its existence and utility, which would help in soliciting their feedback for its evaluation, recommends that model guidelines may be framed by the Ministry of Personnel and given
to all the Ministries/Departments/Organisations so that the mode of receiving feedback would be uniform.
(para 12.1.1)
 
The Committee, thus, desires that the States which has not informed the steps taken by them in this regard to the Ministry, may be required to do so in a time- bound manner.
(para 12.1.2)
 
In the Action Taken Replies to the observations/recommendations contained in the   Seventy-first Report of the Committee, the Ministry had simply stated that the observations/recommendations of the Committee has been communicated to the Nodal Officers for Citizens’ Charters of all the
Ministries/Departments of Central Government and also to the Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all States/UT Governments on 25.05.01 for compliance.  The Ministry has further stated, that they have been requested to ensure that the Charter movement in their organisation is given adequate
publicity and is properly implemented.  They have been requested to evolve a feed back mechanism with participation from the representatives of the people.  This Committee is not happy the way the Ministry intends to comply with the observations/recommendations of the Committee.  The
Ministry has not stated clearly its own monitoring of the instructions/guidelines issued to different agencies under Central and State/ UT Governments.  The Ministry should have evolved a time-frame within which these agencies should have given feed back to the Ministry in compliance of its
instructions/guidelines.  As stated by the Ministry, the instructions/guidelines were issued in May 2001.  But nothing has been stated in the ATR as to what actual action has been taken by these agencies till the time of submission of the ATR to the Committee.  It appears that the Ministry intends
to avoid its responsibility.  It intends to confine its activity by merely issuing guidelines/instructions without caring for their proper compliance.  This attitude of the Ministry is bound to defeat the spirit of the observations/recommendations of the Committee.  This Committee therefore urges upon
the Ministry to submit to it the results of their monitoring of Citizen’s Charter.
(para 12.2)
 
INFORMATION AND FACILITATION COUNTERS
 
During the examination of Demands for Grants (2001-2002), it was intimated to the Committee that only three organisations having Citizen’s Charter had not set up IFCs.  The increase in number of organisations for setting up IFCs from 3 to 21 shows that the Department of Administrative
Reforms is not pursuing the matter vigorously with the latter.  The Committee fails to comprehend as to how the number of Ministries/Departments/Organisations having Citizens’ Charters but have not set up IFCs has increased in the face of tall claim of the Ministry for proper monitoring and
coordination with the Departments/Organisations in the direction of setting up IFCs.  The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that the Government needs to take a serious stand in this regard and that such Ministries/Departments/Organisations may be requested for setting up of IFCs,
as Citizens’ Charter  is meaningless without its physical manifestation.  The Committee further urges upon the Government to monitor each of the Ministries/Departments/Organisations who have not set up IFCs in setting up of their IFCs and render necessary assistance.
(para 13.2.1)
 
In the Action Taken Replies to the observations/recommendations of the Committee as contained in its Seventy-first Report, the Ministry has stated that such Ministries/Departments/Organisations which have Citizens’ Charters but do not have IFCs have been asked to set up IFCs in their
respective organisations throughd.o. letter dated 18June 2001.  However, the Ministry has not stipulated clearly as to what happened to compliance of their D.O. letter.  It gives the impression that either the Ministry does not intend to furnish full facts or is trying to avoid its responsibility of
monitoring the developments in compliance of their instructions/guidelines.  The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to submit a detailed report of monitoring the developments in compliance of their instructions/guidelines every year.
(para 13.2.2)
 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL

This Committee does not understand why the Ministry is trying to evade its responsibility of monitoring its guidelines/instructions in compliance of the observations/recommendations of this Committee.  It is the duty and responsibility of the Ministry to ask different agencies under both Central
and State/UT Governments of the periodic reports of the achievements in quantified terms and to further submit its report to this Committee.  The Ministry is, therefore, directed to do the needful.
(para 14.1)
 
The Committee regards the Action Taken Replies as incomplete and therefore desires that details of all the developments along with the reasons if nothing has been done in this regard in compliance of the observations/recommendations of this Committee, may be furnished to it.
(para 14.3)
 
The Committee, while appreciating the role of the JCM and BoA in solving the cases relating to grievances of Government servants, reiterates its earlier view that these mechanisms may be strengthened for timely redressal of grievances.
(para 14.5.4)
 
The Committee notes the reply and urges upon the Government to continuously strive to identify ways to tackle the whole range of issues for good governance.
(para 14.6.2)
 
The Committee expresses its disappointment over the slow pace of grievance redressal.  It is of the view that the purpose of PGRAMS of speedy redress and effective monitoring of complaints have not been addressed effectively.  It, therefore, recommends to the Government to constantly pursue
the complaints forwarded to Ministries/Department/Organisations/State Governments/UT Administrations for their timely action. It also desires that those officers responsible for making delay in redressal of grievances should be made accountable for that.
(para14.8)
 
VOLUNTARY RETIREMENT SCHEME
 
The Committee feels that the present VRS package has not attracted much attention of employees.  If the Government is seriously considering rightsizing the Government machinery, the Special VRS package needs to be made more attractive and a review thereon may be conducted.
(para 15.4)
CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
 
In view of the above, the Committee desires that immediate action be taken to fill in these vacancies.  It also desires that the Government should make it a point to start initiation of the process for selection of persons to fill in vacancies in CAT at least three months before it occurs in order to
avoid a vacuum in such positions.
(para 16.6)
 
In view of the mounting pendency of cases with CAT and SATs, the Committee fails to understand the reasons for the proposed amendment to do away with the CAT or of SATs.  It, therefore, desires that the Government may first finalise the forum to which these cases are proposed to be
transferred before moving an amendment to liquidate the CAT and SATs.
(para 16.11)
 
The reply of the Ministry is far from satisfactory.  This Committee does not understand why the Ministry takes the plea of the inability of CAT to furnish the requisite information, when the Ministry itself has it.  The Ministry cannot deny that the matters pertaining to JCM and BoA are their
subject-matter and no service –related issues are raised in such bodies without the knowledge of the Ministry. Again, if any such case was to be raised in CAT, it was unlikely that any Official Affidavit (OA) would be filed in any Bench of the CAT without intimating the Ministry as one of the
party/respondent.  The Committee, therefore, directs the Ministry to furnish the details of such information as sought by it.
(para 16.12.1)
 
The Committee is already aware of the facts furnished by the Ministry.  The concern of this Committee is the increasing number of cases pending before the CAT.  As a result, the very purpose of speedy trail and proper dispensation of justice is defeated  This Committee is of the considered view
that the Ministry shall activate these machineries, of JCM and BoA in such a way that maximum number of cases, group or individual are disposed to the satisfaction  of both the parties in the disputes, so that the requirement of going before the CAT would not be felt.  It appears that the Ministry
does not intend to appreciate its responsibilities in this regard and it wants to avoid it. The Ministry is urged to come before the Committee with improvisation of the existing scheme so that there shall be frequent interaction between the authorities concerned and the representatives of the
Government servants at every level of decision making to dispense justice to aggrieved Government employees so as to reduce the possibility of moving to the CAT.
(para 16.12.2)
 
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
 
A perusal of the information furnished by the Government indicates a disheartening pace of clearing pendency.  The Committee, while noting the steps adopted by the Government to dispose of cases under investigation fails to understand as to why only 43 cases are under active investigation out
of the 241 cases pending over 2 years. The Committee therefore urges the Government to seriously monitor the implementation of steps it has framed for itself to expeditiously dispose of cases pending with CBI.
(para 17.8)
The Committee, while appreciating the review to identify the need for more Special Courts, urges the Government to initiate action and extend every possible assistance to the States in setting up of these courts within a set timeframe considering the mounting cases pending with the CBI as this
would go a long way in clearing the arrears of pendency.
(para 17.9.3)
 
While appreciating the proposal of the Government to revise the CBI Crime Manual, the Committee desires that the exercise must be carefully carried out in the light of changing scenario in national and trans-national crimes.
                             (para 17.10.1)
           
The Committee notes the judgement of the Supreme Court with regard to giving consent to CBI to investigate cases by State Governments. 
(para 17.12)
 
The Committee, while noting the above fact feels that the need of the hour is to convert CBI into a computer savvy organization, equipped to deal with the increasingly sensitive matters entrusted to it.  The Committee, however, is of the view that strengthening it by filling up the vacant posts
suitably on deputation would be the first step the Government ought to consider seriously.
(para 17.15)
 
The Committee appreciates the CBI’s proposal of 9.1.2002 that the principle of re-assessment to strengthen the CBI should be finalized in a high level meeting first, it urges the Government to seriously strive to equip CBI and make it competent to new fields like, cyber crime, economic crime. 
Steps should also be taken to enable CBI to function effectively as Federal Police.
(para17.16)
 
The Committee drew the attention of the Ministry to the delay in bringing the Annual Report of CBI as the latest Annual Report of CBI made available to it pertains to the year 1999 and wanted to know the reasons for non-finalisation of Annual Reports for the years 2000 and 2001. The Secretary

The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry.

The Ministry of Home Affairs has been entrusted broadly with the following functions:
            (a)        To deal with all matters relating to internal security;
(b)        To deal with all matters relating to Centre-State relations and Inter-State relations;
(c)        Implementation of the provisions of the Constitution relating to Official Language and the provisions of
the Official Language Act, 1963;
(d)        To discharge certain basic functions like notification of assumption of office by the President and the
Vice-President; notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers; notification of
appointment, resignation and removal of Governors and Lt. Governors, appointment of Lt. Governors,
Chief Commissioners and Administrative Officers in Union Territories;
(e)        To deal with matters like citizenship and naturalisation, census of population, National Anthem, National
Flag, etc.; and
(f)         To deal with all constitutional provisions with respect to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and all other
matters relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding those with which the Ministry of External
Affairs is concerned.
2.         To discharge the above functions, the Ministry has been divided into five Departments:
(i)         Department of Internal Security – to deal with Police, Law and Order and rehabilitation;
(ii)        Department of States – to deal with Centre-State relations, inter-State relations, Union Territories and
Freedom Fighters’ Pension;

relating to Official Language and provisions of the Official Language Act, 1963;
(iv)       Department of Home – to deal with notification of assumption of office by the President and Vice-
President, notification of appointment of the Prime Minister and other Ministers, etc.; and
(v)        Department of Jammu and Kashmir Affairs – to deal with all constitutional provisions with respect to the
State of Jammu and Kashmir and all other matters relating to the State of Jammu and Kashmir excluding
those with which the Ministry of External Affairs is concerned.

12.       Demand Nos. 98, 99, 100, 101 and 102 which are given in Volume-II of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry
of Home Affairs, relate to Union Territories (without Legislature), namely Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh,
Dadra & Nagar Haveli, Daman & Diu and Lakshadweep, respectively. The entire budget of the Union Territories
(without Legislature) on the Plan as well as Non-Plan side is reflected in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry. Though
the budget of these Union Territories forms part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, being the nodal Ministry, it, however,
does not dilute the responsibilities of the Ministries of the Central Government from scrutinising and sanctioning the
schemes under their purview. The factual position regarding budgetary procedure in this regard is that the entire budget
requirement for Plan and Non-Plan, revised estimates for current year and Non-Plan budget estimates for the ensuing year
is discussed by the Ministry of Finance in the pre-budget meetings with the representatives of the concerned Union
Territories and Ministry of Home Affairs. An overall ceiling is fixed in respect of each Union Territory. The Planning
Commission decides annual Plan allocations for the ensuing year. The Union Territory Administrations prepare budgetary
break-up showing budget provisions according to their respective budgetary heads and also showing the allocation against
Ministries/Departments of the Central Government administratively concerned. This budgetary break-up is included in
the Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
PRESENTATION OF HOME SECRETARY ON DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2002-2003)
13.       The Committee considered the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in its meetings held on 2,3,4 and 5 April
2002.  The Home Secretary made a presentation before the Committee on 5 April  2002 with the help of audio-visual
means.
14.       The Home Secretary began his presentation with an overview of internal security situation in the country.  He
apprised the Committee about the progress made on various fronts and the steps and measures taken last year.  He stated
that there were three high points on the graph of terrorism during the year 2001 namely, 11
th September attack on World
Trade Centre and Pentagon in the USA, 1 st October attack on Jammu & Kashmir Legislative Assembly and 13 th
December attack on the Parliament House. He stated that before 11 th September, India’s position regarding Pakistan
sponsored terrorism was accepted in the international forums grudgingly or with skepticism. However, this single event
not only globalized the fight against terrorism but had found India partners in its over decade-old struggle. He further
stated that the attacks on the Parliament House and the Jammu & Kashmir Legislative Assembly were not ordinary
terrorist assaults. These were in the nature of spectacular strikes on the two hubs of Indian democracy, throwing a direct
challenge to the Government of India. The events of the last year had also revived the threat of the likely use of weapons
of mass destruction against the civilized world. He informed the Committee that it was reliably known that certain
terrorist outfits  already possessed some of these weapons or were capable of acquiring them. As a result of which the
threats to internal security from terrorism of various forms – conventional, cyber, nuclear, biological and chemical – were
real and grave and it would not be prudent to take these threats lightly or casually. It would, therefore, be advisable to
take precautions and be ready for all contingencies. He apprised the Committee that in accordance with such threat
perceptions, a total review of the existing disaster prevention and management systems was under way, in consultation
with the State Governments, to locate gaps and deficiencies therein and to initiate a process of filling the gaps and
correcting the deficiencies so identified. He stated that it had already been decided to transfer the subject of disaster
management – except management of droughts and famines – from the Ministry of Agriculture to the Ministry of Home
Affairs. In this regard, a detailed proposal defining structures required for disaster prevention, management and relief was
being prepared and would be submitted shortly for the approval of the Cabinet. He touched upon the minimum action
programme suggested to the States for revamping their machinery for disaster management.
14.1    The Home Secretary, while referring to the communal violence in Gujarat, stated that the visage of the year 2002
got scarred by the unprecedented communal violence in Gujarat which left nearly 760 persons dead and nearly 1900

88th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/88threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:51:18]
injured. The number of persons rendered homeless was around 98000. He stated that there was, however, a silver lining
that while incidents of communal clashes continued in Gujarat, bandhs organized in various other States passed off
almost peacefully so did the Shiladaan ceremony at Ayodhya on 15 March 2002. 
15.       Thereafter, the Home Secretary gave a detailed description of the internal security trends in vulnerable and
sensitive parts of the country.
16.       With regard to the situation in Jammu & Kashmir, the Home Secretary stated that between 1990 and 2001 the
proxy war unleashed by Pakistan in Jammu & Kashmir had consumed nearly 27500 lives in 52000 incidents. Out of
27500 deaths, 10000 were civilians, 3000 security personnel and 14500 terrorists. During this period of 12 years,
terrorists destroyed 633 educational buildings, 333 bridges, 11 hospitals, 1134 Government buildings, 10263 private
houses and 1932 shops. The graph of terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir showed an increasing trend between 1990 and 1996.
After that it started decreasing which continued till 2000. He further submitted that last year there was an upsurge in
terrorist activities registering 4522 incidents compared to 3074 incidents in 2000. This upsurge could be partly ascribed to
the one-sided cease fire declared by the Government of India in November, 2000 and partly to the fact that the terrorists
were getting desperate under pressure of the Pakistani establishment on the one-side and of the Indian security forces on
the other. As a result, 919 civilians and 536 security personnel lost their lives during 2001. He stated that the Ramzan
peace initiative announced on 27 November 2000 by the Government of India had to be withdrawn on 31 May 2001 after
a patient and testing wait of six months. He further elaborated that during 2001 two features of terrorism in Jammu &
Kashmir became particularly noticeable. One, the attacks were more focused on the security forces and their
establishments and second, that the number of suicide attacks was on the increase. Last year there were 25 fidayeen
(suicide) attacks. This apart, terrorists had also tried to provoke communal feelings by holding up in mosques  hoping that
people would react if security forces attacked the mosques to dislodge the terrorists. However, such tactics had failed. He
informed that there was attack on Amarnath Yatris for second consecutive year. 
16.1     The Home Secretary informed that in addition to six districts of Kashmir Division, all districts of Jammu Division
were declared as ‘disturbed’ areas in 2001 by the Government of Jammu & Kashmir.  He stated that terrorist groups not
only continued to operate from Pakistani soil but also continued to get assistance from the ISI and the Pakistani army.
Contrary to its promises, Pakistan had done nothing to effectively restrict the movement, funding, training or recruitment
of terrorism. All important terrorist organizations, including those which were banned by Pakistan, continued to have
offices not only in Pakistan occupied Kashmir (PoK) but also in Pakistan. In order to deceive the international
community, the banned terrorist organizations had been re-christened   like Lashkar-e-Toiba was now known as Pasban-
e-Ahle Hadith and Jaish-e-Mohammed as Tehrik-ul-Furkan. However, within Jammu & Kashmir, they continued to use
their original names. Referring to the Government’s present strategy in Jammu & Kashmir, he stated that besides taking
on the terrorist outfits in a direct combat, it was focused on further deepening of democratic process and sustenance of
developmental process over a period of time so that public opinion and energy were mobilized against terrorism.
17.       While apprising the Committee of the situation in North-East, the Home Secretary stated that the level of violence
in the region had declined, though the internal security situation particularly in the States of Assam, Manipur and Tripura
continued to be disturbed. There were also disturbing signs of an upswing in violence in Meghalaya and Arunachal
Pradesh. During the year 2001, there were 1339 incidents of violence compared with 1963 incidents in 2000. During
2001, 600 civilians and 175 security personnel were killed in terrorist violence as against the figures of 907 civilians and
164 security personnel during 2000. Last year 572 militants were killed compared to 584 killed the year before. Arms
looted by militants were 111 in 2001 as compared to 216 in 2000. The number of arms recovered was 577 in 2001 as
compared to 574 in 2000. He stated that most serious incidents of violence took place in Manipur in the aftermath of the
announcement of extension of ceasefire agreement between the Government of India and the NSCN (IM) without
territorial limits in the North-East. The announcement evoked widespread resentment in Manipur as also in Assam and
Arunachal Pradesh. In deference to the public sentiments, the Government announced restoration of status quo ante which
led to the return of normalcy. The cause of such unprecedented violence lay in the apprehension in the minds of the
people of Manipur that the extension of ceasefire to their areas might lead to a territorial division of this State at some
point of time in future. Referring to the talks with NSCN (IM), the Home Secretary informed that the talks on substantive
issues had already begun with NSCN (IM). A set of demands received from the NSCN (IM) was under consideration of
the Government. He further stated that the Government of India entered into a formal ceasefire with the NSCN (K) for a
period of one year w.e.f. 28 April 2001 on persistent demands of the Government of Nagaland, NGOs and Church
leaders. He hoped that the signing of the ceasefire agreement would enlarge the area of peace in Nagaland. As regards the
talks with Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) in Assam, he stated that talks with that group were continuing and the level of
violence attributable to this militant outfit had come down substantially.

17.1     He informed that an amount of Rs. 139.77 crore  had been released as Security Related Expenditure (SRE) during
the financial year 2001-2002. Sharing his anxiety, the Home Secretary stated that an understanding and nexus was
emerging among the militant outfits active in Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland and Tripura. This was partly on account of
the compulsion of these outfits for alternative sanctuaries and camps and partly on account of their need for weapons and
training. He assured the Committee that the Government had taken note of this development for being factored into its
strategy for the North-East.
18.       With regard to left wing extremism, the Home Secretary stated that the magnitude as well as the intensity of left
wing extremist violence registered an upsurge for the first time since 1996 with 1208 incidents and 564 deaths reported
during 2001. In 2000, the number of incidents was 1179 and number of lives lost 550. States of Andhra Pradesh,
Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh witnessed a spurt in naxalite violence while there was a comparative decline in Bihar. There
was also a significant increase in the level of naxalite violence in States of Madhya Pradesh and Orrisa. He submitted that
there were sure signs that left wing extremism was spreading its tentacles in the States of Uttar Pradesh and West
Bengal.   He informed that Andhra Pradesh accounted for a larger proportion of naxalite violence as compared to Bihar
and Jharkhand. There was steep escalation in attacks on Government and private properties with the CPML-PW resorting
to attacks on the private property of high profile targets. He further stated that the declaration of ceasefire between
CPML-PW and the MCC during the year 2001 was an ominous development as it could lead to further escalation of
violence against State apparatus and a further expansion and consolidation of the movement in Bihar, Jharkhand and other
adjoining States. The Home Secretary while sharing his concern with the Committee, stated that the Compact
Revolutionary Zone (CRZ) envisaged by the MCC, the CPML-PW and the CPN (Maoist) for linking up the strongholds
of the CPML-PW in Telengana and Dandkaranya and of the MCC in Bihar and Jharkhand with those of the CPN (Maoist)
in Nepal by cutting across Chhattisgarh continued to be a live concern. Of further concern was the consolidation of
naxalite influence in areas contiguous to the CRZ in Eastern U.P., North Orrisa and West-Bengal thereby leading to a
naxalite buffer zone around the CRZ that could ultimately facilitate its expansion sideways. The threat of CRZ had
assumed greater gravity in the light of the heightened Maoist violence in Nepal. He informed that the States affected by
left wing   extremism had been fully sensitized about these latest developments and also advised to take suitable action
against the emergence and consolidation of CRZ.  He further informed that the States of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh were
also made members of the Coordination Centre set up to deal with the problem of left wing extremism. This Coordination
Centre had been concentrating both on the security and development options of dealing with left wing extremism. He
apprised the Committee that the Coordination Centre reviewed the existing and emerging security scenarios from time to
time and modified and fine tuned the security strategy according to the requirement of the ground situation. The Home
Secretary informed that the scheme of reimbursement of security related expenditure, which was valid till 31 March 2001,
had since been extended for another five years.    
19.       In relation to the situation in Punjab, the Home Secretary stated that though there was no incident of violence in
Punjab in 2001 as against five major incidents and 20 deaths in 2000, the recent inputs indicated that Pakistan-based
terrorists of Khalistan Commando Force (Panjwar), Babbar Khalsa International, Khalistan Jindabad Force and
International Sikh Youth Federation (Rode) were desperate to undertake some sensational terrorist action in India because
of constant pressure from the Pak-ISI. Attempts   to resurrect terrorism in Punjab also became evident from the continued
recovery of large quantity of arms, ammunition, explosives and sophisticated timer devices in Punjab. The security forces
arrested 31 terrorists while one surrendered before the police during 2001 as against 35 terrorists arrested and 3
surrendered in the year 2000. The Home Secretary cautioned that  despite the reverses and neutralisation of some of their
top rung activists over the years, the Khalistani terrorist still retained the capacity and substantial fire power to carry out
acts of violence. Therefore, it would be equally important to guard against any nexus between Khalistani and Kashmiri
terrorist groups. 
20.       Touching upon the situation in the capital city of Delhi, the Home Secretary informed that the capital’s crime
graph had shown a consistent increase till the year 1998 and started showing declining trend in the year 1999. This
downward trend continued during the year 2001 also. Besides, Delhi Police had in the last two years achieved significant
successes in controlling the activities of various terrorist organizations, inter-state gangsters and the Mumbai underworld
in Delhi. During the year 2001, Delhi Police arrested or killed 56 terrorists belonging to JKLF, Al Qaeda, Harkat-ul-
Jehad-e-Islami, Hizbul Muzahideen, SIMI, Lashkar-e-Toiba and Jaish-e-Mohammad. This included 5 terrorists who were
killed in a fierce gun battle inside the Parliament House Complex and 4 of their accomplices arrested during the course of
investigation. Special  security arrangements in the highly sensitive areas covering important Government buildings was
also put in place. The security arrangements inside and around the Parliament House had also been reviewed and
strengthened in the aftermath of terrorist attack.

20.1     Referring to the BPR&D’s report on manpower requirements and modernization needs of Delhi Police, the Home

requirements of Delhi Police. Accordingly, Delhi Police had been advised to prioritise its requirements and send

21.       In relation to communal violence, the Home Secretary stated that a declining trend in Hindu-Muslim communal
violence for eight consecutive years was arrested in 2001 when an upward trend became discernible. The year 2001
registered 617 incidents in which 199 persons got killed and 2066 injured. Nearly 90% of the communal incidents were
reported from the States of Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar, West-

21.1     The Home Secretary further stated that the year 2002  started on a bad note  so far as communal harmony and

of India (SIMI) were banned under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. The ban on both the organizations

Kamtapur and a separate Gorkhaland did not witness much agitation. Agrarian situation, by and large remained peaceful.

consideration, the Home Secretary apprised it of major policy initiatives taken during the year 2001. 
26.1     He informed the Committee that the report of the Group of Ministers (GoM) on National Security was considered
and accepted by the Government in May 2001.  The process of implementation of the recommendations of the GoM had
been set in motion and was being closely monitored at the level of Cabinet Secretary.    The recommendations pertained
to the areas of intelligence apparatus, internal security, border management and defence.  The Ministry of Home Affairs
was concerned with the first three and the recommendations pertaining to these were at various stages of implementation. 
While giving an outline of major recommendations of GoM, the Home Secretary stated that the areas of  ‘intelligence
apparatus’ included the establishment of an Intelligence Coordination Group (ICG) and a Technology Coordination
Group (TCG) working in close tandem with National Technical Facility Organisation (NTFO).  Giving details of each of
these groups, the Home Secretary stated that ICG would provide for systematic intelligence oversight mechanism at the
apex level and inter alia deal with (i) annual tasking for intelligence collection; (ii) overseeing the functioning of
intelligence agencies; (iii) reviewing annually the quality of inputs; and (iv) allocating resources to intelligence agencies. 
On the other hand, TCG would coordinate and regulate plans for acquisition of all new, expensive or major strategic
facilities and equipment by the intelligence agencies.  It would generally oversee their TECHINT capabilities and also
examine issues relating to the allocations of fund for this purpose.  NTFO would inter alia plan, design, set up and operate
new strategic and expensive TECHINT facilities as approved by TCG keeping in view the rapid convergence now taking
place among hitherto different technologies.  The Home Secretary further informed that the GoM had recommended
constitution of Joint Task Force on Intelligence and a Multi-Agency Centre in the Intelligence Bureau Headquarters as
well as Inter-State Intelligence Support Teams and Multi-Agency Centres in the States also under the aegis of the
Intelligence Bureau, to ensure better coordination between the Central and the State intelligence agencies.
26.1.1  As regards border management, the Home Secretary informed that it was to be refashioned on a ‘one border- one
force’ principle so as to obviate problems of conflict in command and control and lack of accountability arising from the

not to be withdrawn as a rule for internal security or counter insurgency duties.  These border-guarding forces were also
to be appropriately strengthened, trained and equipped with weapons on par with related army units when deployed on
similar tasks.  Similarly, the Coast Guard was also to be strengthened and a specialized Marine Police to be raised in all
coastal States and island territories.  The border guarding forces were also required to function as the Lead Intelligence
Agencies for border areas.
26.1.2  Referring to the recommendations of GoM in regard to the maintenance of internal security, the Home Secretary
stated that in pursuance of the recommendations of GoM, the State Police and Central Para Military Forces were to be
modernized particularly in respect of weapon systems, equipment and training.  The Central forces would be supported by
a rejuvenated Civil Defence Organisation, Village and Ward Defence Committees and a revamped criminal justice system
backed by laws and regulations appropriate to emerging circumstances.  He further stated that the proposed new
structures would anticipate current and emerging security threats, be they nuclear, cyber, technological or from
international terrorism, low intensity conflict and proxy war.  There would be new and innovative organizational
platforms capable of flexible responses and not just upgradations of existing systems.  He hoped that the participation of
key political players, namely, National Security Adviser, Cabinet Secretary, the Services, Para Military Forces, Police and
Intelligence Chiefs and the Principal Scientific Advisor to the Government in the entire exercise would ensure the
necessary political will, financial commitment and operational back-up to secure what constituted a ‘radical systemic
change’.
26.2     While apprising the Committee of a number of decisions and actions taken by the Government flowing from the
recommendations of GoM, the Home Secretary stated that it had been decided to raise 209 battalions comprising 26
battalions of BSF, 84 battalions of CRPF, 10 battalions of Assam Rifles, 9 battalions of ITBP, 50 India Reserve battalions
and 30 battalions of Rashtriya Rifles in a phased manner by 2004-2005. With these additional raisings, it was expected
that the border guarding forces would not normally have to be withdrawn from their primary duties and the CRPF would
be able to cope with the demands of the States for aid in the event of serious breach of public order and peace.  According
to the timetable, 42 battalions were to be raised during 2001-2002 for which necessary sanctions had since been issued.
He further informed that the target for the year 2002-2003 was to raise 45 battalions. Referring to the modernization plan
of Central Para Military Forces, the Home Secretary stated that it had been approved and was expected to cost Rs.3740.71
crore over five years.  The modernization programme would ensure upgradation of weapon systems, communication
systems, surveillance systems, and training infrastructure and also meet other critical requirements of these forces.  He
informed that a Committee had been set up to assess and evaluate the modernization needs of Central Para Military
Forces on a continuing basis.  He further informed that a proposal to renew and modernize the air wing of BSF at an
estimated cost of Rs.589.42 crore had also been approved.  The procurement of six new aircraft to replace six old aircrafts
would be completed over a period of two years. 
26.2.1  The Home Secretary stated that a new Border Management Division had been created in the Ministry of Home
Affairs which would pay focused attention to the issues pertaining to effective border management of the country.  He
submitted that this Division would grow, in due course, into a Department of Border Management as per the
recommendation of GoM.  He informed that the Special Service Bureau had been placed under the administrative control
of Ministry of Home Affairs and had been deployed in selected vulnerable stretches of Indo-Nepal Border.  As regards
operational efficiency of Central Para Military Forces, he stated that intelligence units at battalion and unit levels had
been set up in all Central Para Military Forces.  The Government had nominated the principal border guarding force as
the lead intelligence agency for the respective borders.  The lead intelligence agency had been tasked to be the
intelligence wing responsible for coordinating the activities of all agencies which operated in that segment of the border

institutions.  That Committee had identified the requirements of additional infrastructure and manpower in respect of each
designated Centre of Excellence.  It was proposed to meet these requirements over a period of three years at an estimated
cost of Rs.85 crore.   It had also been decided to prescribe benchmarks of standardization so that these centres could be
compared with the international training institutions in their respective fields of specialization.  The aim was to expose the
trainees to international standards of training as far as possible.

28.1     While sharing his interaction with DGPs and IGPs of the States in their annual conference held in September
2001, the Home Secretary stated that he had pointedly asked them to make the police station, centre of all reform and
modernization efforts.  He was of the view that benefit of additional funds under the scheme for modernization of police
forces should first and foremost go to the police station, the cutting edge of governance and of public-police interface. 
Accordingly, he had advised the DGPs and IGPs to transform their police stations over the next ten years into model and
modern work places which were staffed with pleasant, positive and sympathetic personnel.  He believed that such a
transformation would come about mainly with attitudinal changes right down to the level of police constable.  Keeping
this in view, the Home Secretary had requested the DGPs and IGPs to take personal interest in re-orienting the training
regimen of their men and officers.  The States were also advised to accord due weightage in their perspective plans to the
strengthening of intelligence gathering machinery.  The intelligence gathering machinery had not been as sharp, vigilant
and ruthless as it should be largely because of unwillingness of police personnel to join the Special Branch.  Accordingly,

30.       Referring to the need for an anti-terrorism law, the Home Secretary stated that after the lapse of TADA in 1995,
there was a general consensus that there should be an anti-terrorism law with adequate safeguards against its possible
misuse for harassing innocent people.  Keeping these parameters in view, the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance 2000
was promulgated on 24 October 2001.  Since the Bill to replace the ordinance could not be introduced in the Lok Sabha,
the second ordinance was promulgated on 30 December 2001.  This ordinance had since been legislated by  Parliament
and had also received the assent of the President.  The Home Secretary informed that keeping in view the apprehensions
about the possible misuse of provisions of this law, State Governments had been advised to install a suitable mechanism
to oversee its fair and transparent implementation.
31.       The Home Secretary, in his concluding remarks, stated that India had faced and fought terrorism for over two
decades during which many lessons had been learnt.  Two most important things for a terrorist movement to die down
were that it should lose public support as well as its financial base because without these two, no militancy could survive
for long.  He stated that since many members of terrorist outfits were our own people, albeit misguided ones, we could
not think of destroying them like the USA did to the Taliban and the Al Qaeda.  Nor a religious war was being waged. 
The war was between all sane and peace loving people of the country against the enemies of peace, progress and
development.  He submitted that all strategies were based on this premise and that is why they were long-drawn and also
met more obstacles than a normal military strategy.  He exuded the confidence that with patience and perseverance
backed up by the courage and bravery of our forces and the indomitable will and yearning of Indian people for peace, we
should be able to restore peace, tranquility and prosperity in the areas which had been ravaged by violence and strife of
one kind or the other.  He sought the valued advice and guidance of the Committee in fulfilling this resolve.

LEFT WING EXTREMISM
43.       Left wing extremism has been posing one of the biggest challenges on the internal security front.  Several States,
namely, Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and two of newly
created States of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh have been bearing the brunt of violence unleashed by the protagonists of
this kind of extremism viz. CPML-PW and MCC.  These groups have been making concerted efforts to militarise their
cadres through formation of special guerilla squads and extend their activities over larger areas of the country.  Not just
that, they are now forging links with Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist).  These groups have even envisaged a Compact
Revolutionary Zone (CRZ) by linking up their strongholds spread across Telangana, Dandkaranya, Bihar, Jharkhand and
Chhattisgarh in India and areas of influence of Communist Party of Nepal (CPN-Maoist).  The violence unleashed by
these extremist groups has seen an upsurge in 2001 after having been in doldrums since 1996.  The Ministry of Home
Affairs has informed that some of the violent incidents occurred in 2001, were due to the protest actions of PWG and
MCC for declaring them as terrorist organizations under the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance, 2001. 
43.1     In reply to a query as to what measures had been taken to quell the spurt in the violence, the Ministry of Home
Affairs replied that ‘Public Order’ and ‘Police’ being State subjects, it was for the concerned State Governments to devise
various methods and take concrete steps to curb left wing extremist activities in the States.  However, keeping in view the
overall dimensions of left wing extremism, a Coordination Centre headed by the Union Home Secretary with Chief
Secretaries and Directors General of Police of the seriously affected States, as its members, regularly reviewed and
coordinated steps taken by the States to check left wing extremist activities, monitored the plan of action in respect of
each State and made recommendations both on development and security aspects of the problem.  Several important
decisions such as providing financial support from the Central Government for combating left wing extremist activities,
preparation of plans for development of affected areas, to tackle the problem in a holistic manner, sharing of intelligence
inputs, and providing assistance of para military forces on need basis, etc. had been taken by the Coordination Centre and
effectively followed-up.  CPML-Peoples War (PW) and Maoist Communist Centre (MCC) and their formations and front
organizations had been notified as Terrorist Organisations under the provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism (Second)
Ordinance 2001 to enable the States to take effective action against them.  In order to curb Maoist activities on the Indian
soil along Indo-Nepal Border, Special Service Bureau (SSB) personnel had been deployed in the border States of
Uttaranchal, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal covering the districts of Pithoragarh, Champawat, Udham Singh
Nagar of Uttaranchal, Pilibhit and part of Lakhimpur Kheri of Uttar Pradesh, Purbi Champaran, Madhubani, Piprakoti,
Kishanganj, Sitamarhi, Supaul of Bihar and Darjeeling in West Bengal.  State Governments had also been advised to gear
up their intelligence machinery for collection and sharing of intelligence from the field, particularly with regard to
possible plans of sympathizers of CPN (M) to hold meetings, raise funds and organize logistic support.  States had also
been advised that any attempts of Maoist elements to seek sanctuary would have to be firmly deterred and a close watch
kept on movement of arms, ammunition and explosives to and from Nepal.
43.2     The Home Secretary, in his presentation before the Committee, also informed that the magnitude as well as the
intensity of left wing extremist violence registered an upsurge for the first time since 1996 with 1208 incidents and 564

MONSTER OF COMMUNALISM
45.       Communalism has been the bane of modern India.  It acted as a midwife in the partition of India and even after
that it continues to plague the social fabric of the country.  It has acquired different forms and dimensions over the years. 
However, in the recent years it is rearing its ugly head in an organized manner much in the same way as it did in the years
preceding the partition.  There are several forces which work tirelessly to ensure that it does not lose it momentum.  These
forces are the real anti-national elements who are bent upon tearing the social fabric of the nation apart.  In their zeal to
gain foothold in their respective communities, these forces are stoking communal fire.  Their actions are spreading venom
in the society which threatens to be divided along communal lines.  These attempts to create a communal divide in the
society are one of the biggest challenges before the Indian polity.  Therefore, it needs to be nipped in the bud before it
grows too large to be controlled.  It is the considered view of this Committee that the Government must make honest and
sincere efforts to maintain the pluralistic character of the society and bring all right thinking elements of all communities
together to try and find ways to check the growing divide between them.
POLITICISATION OF POLICE FORCES
46.       Indian police system is a relic of the British colonialism.  Various Commissions and Committees set up from time
to time to suggest the measures necessary to purge the system have come out with a plethora of suggestions and
recommendations.  These recommendations have not at all been implemented  by some States and where they have been
implemented their letter and spirit has not been followed.  As a result of that, Indian police system continues to be
plagued by several ills.  Some of these ills were inherited by it from its colonial masters while some have crept into it as it
has evolved in the post-colonial period.  In the post-colonial period, it has been made to subserve the ruling elite.  This
has   raised  a  big  question mark over the  objectivity and
impartiality of the police.  Today we have a police which is politicized and politically polarized.  For it has become a
pawn in the hands of its masters.  In return, policemen get political patronage which has become essential for their
survival.  These days police personnel are found to be divided in camps with each camp having its own political leanings. 
This connivance of the police with the powers that be is giving rise to cynicism among people who are not only losing
faith in the police but also in the democratic principles of our polity.  These are, by all means, very dangerous signs for
the continuance and survival of democracy.  What can be more dangerous than a situation when people are losing faith in
as vital an institution as the police?
47.       In this backdrop, the Committee feels that there is need for a serious introspection by all concerned.  The
Government must act fast to stem the rot which has set in.  If immediate steps are not taken to set the house in order, there
are dangers of the system falling prey to these degenerating developments.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Government should make earnest efforts to depoliticise the institution of police before it becomes too late to retrieve it
from the morass of degeneration.  It must be ensured that police remains accountable only to the law of the land.

modernization of police forces is the primary responsibility of the State Governments.  However, the Central Government

police forces.  For, an efficient and modernized police is a sine qua non for proper maintenance of internal security.  With

REVAMP OF INTELLIGENCE APPARATUS
51.       Large scale intrusion of foreign mercenaries and Pak army regulars in Kargil in 1999 woke up the Indian
establishment to the need for a systemic overhaul of the intelligence set up.  Intrusions in Kargil proved a watershed
development for the overhaul of intelligence apparatus.  In the aftermath of Kargil war, a Group of Ministers (GoM) on
National Security was constituted to deliberate upon various issues and questions relating to the national security in a
comprehensive manner.  The report of the GoM was considered and accepted by the Government in May 2001.  The
Report focused on the areas of intelligence apparatus, internal security, border management and defence.  As regards
intelligence apparatus, the GOM has recommended the setting up of an Intelligence Coordination Group (ICG), a
Technology Coordination Group (TCG) and a National Technical Facility Organisation (NTFO).  The establishment of
these groups is aimed at ensuring better flow of intelligence inputs and providing strategic facilities and equipment.  In
addition to this, the GoM has also recommended the constitution of a Joint Task Force on Intelligence and a Multi-
Agency Centre in the Intelligence Bureau Headquarters as well as Inter-State Intelligence Support Teams and Multi-
Agency Centres in the States under the aegis of the Intelligence Bureau.  This entire paraphernalia is being put in place to
see that intelligence apparatus of the country is fully geared up, equipped and vigilant to ward off the nefarious designs of
divisive forces and the enemies.
52.       The Committee is satisfied to note the steps being taken to revamp the entire intelligence apparatus.  It hopes that
the new set-up will function smoothly.  However, with too many groups and agencies entrusted with different aspects of
intelligence, the real problem arises in regard to proper coordination amongst all of them.  The Committee hopes that all

set its sinister designs against India into motion, it has spun a web of its operatives across the length and breadth of the
country.  These operatives with the help of their local connections work ceaselessly not just to foment trouble but also to
aid and abet troublemakers.  As part of this strategy, ISI is providing financial assistance towards setting up of religious
fundamentalist institutions along Indo-Nepal border.  These institutions not only provide safe sanctuaries to ISI’s
handpicked men but also indoctrinate young minds to wage a holy war against India.  In other words, these institutions
have become breeding ground for anti-India elements.  The Ministry of Home Affairs, in response to a query as to

ISI-backed religious institutions/ organizations along Indo-Nepal border.  Some of these institutions were reportedly
being misused by ISI activists for subversive activities against India.

call of the ISI to destabilize India.  The audacity with which ISI is using both Indian people and soil, that too for
destabilizing and disintegrating India, is really condemnable.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to
leave no stone unturned to root out such institutions and the activists being harboured by them   before any irreparable
damage is caused to the unity and integrity of India.

contained in BPR&D’s report, it has not carried out any exercise to work out the cost of their implementation.  It has
merely stated that it would entail huge expenditure.  Similarly, it has not set any timeframe for the implementation of the
report.  By stating that the accepted recommendations would be implemented in a phased manner over a reasonable
period of time, the Ministry has given the impression that it seems to be groping in the dark.
64.       The manner in which the Ministry of Home Affairs is dealing with BPR&D’s report raises serious doubts over its
intentions vis-à-vis the implementation  of the report.  If the Ministry was really sincere about the implementation of the
report, it should have chalked out a concrete timeframe for its implementation after working out costs of its
implementation.  Instead, it has dropped the ball once again in the court of Delhi Police.  The whole exercise appears to
be aimed at putting the implementation of the report on the backburner.  In view of this, the Committee reiterates its
earlier recommendation as contained in its 73
rd Report that the Ministry of Home Affairs should first set a definite
timeframe within which the recommendations of BPR&D will be implemented.  Similarly, the estimated costs of
implementation of the recommendations should be worked out and necessary budgetary provisions be earmarked over the
period of implementation of the recommendations.
65.       While going into the details of traffic management in Delhi during the examination of Demands for Grants (2001-
2002), the Committee, in its 73 rd Report thereon, had recommended for setting up of a Unified Traffic Management
Authority in Delhi.  The Ministry of Home Affairs had referred the recommendations to the Government of NCT of Delhi
for obtaining their considered views to enable it to take the decision in the matter in its proper perspective.  In reply to a
query as to what follow up action had been taken by the Government of NCT of Delhi in regard to the setting up of the
recommended authority, the Ministry of Home Affairs informed that the Government of NCT of Delhi had with regard to
the recommendations for setting up of a Unified Transport Management Authority, informed that it was not possible for
them under the existing frame-work to bring about an integrated legislation for setting up of a Unified Transport
Management Authority as Delhi Legislative Assembly was not empowered to legislate with respect to matters connected
with “Police” and “Land”.  The Ministry further informed that it had, however, accepted the recommendation made by
BPR&D in its study report for setting up of a Traffic Advisory Committee under the Chairmanship of the Commissioner
of Police with the representatives drawn from the Government of NCT of Delhi, local bodies and Delhi Development
Authority to continuously monitor such aspects of road engineering and road furniture as help smooth flow of traffic.
66.       The proposal to set up a Traffic Advisory Committee under the Chairmanship of Commissioner of Police, Delhi
falls short of an independent Traffic Management Authority.  The idea behind setting up of such an authority was to
ensure that traffic management was viewed with an integrated approach.  However, that idea seems to have not gone
down well with the policy makers of the Ministry of Home Affairs.  By linking it with a somewhat identical
recommendation as contained in the report of BPR&D, the Ministry has sought to put the setting up of the authority also
on the backburner.  Therefore, the Committee strongly reiterates its earlier recommendation as contained in its 73
rd
Report that the Government should set up a Unified Traffic Management Authority vested with the powers of overall
planning and management of traffic in Delhi.
67.       The satisfaction level of residential accommodation for the personnel of Delhi Police continues to be static
primarily because of the inability of the PWD of Government of NCT of Delhi to satisfactorily cater to the requirements
of Delhi Police because of their commitments elsewhere.  To overcome this hurdle in raising the satisfaction level, the
Committee had recommended for setting up of a Housing Corporation for Delhi Police.  As the proposal did not find
favour with the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Committee endorsed the proposal of the Ministry to carve out a separate
dedicated wing out of the PWD to cater to the housing needs of Delhi Police.  However, this proposal too could not

therefore, urges upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to come out with some concrete proposals to raise the housing
satisfaction level of Delhi Police in the next couple of years to a fairly satisfactory level.
SITUATION IN PUNJAB
68.       The Home Secretary, in his presentation, apprised the Committee that the recent inputs indicated that Pak based
terrorists of Khalistan Commando Force (Panjwar), Babbar Khalsa International, Khalistan Zindabad Force and
International Sikh Youth Federation (Rode) were desperate to undertake some sensational terrorist action in India because
of constant pressure from Pak ISI.  Attempts to resurrect terrorism in Punjab also became evident from the continued
recovery of large quantities of arms, ammunition, explosives and sophisticated timer devices in the State.  He informed
that the security forces arrested 31 terrorists while one surrendered before the police in 2001.  Similarly, 35 terrorists were
arrested and 3 surrendered in 2000.  He further stated that despite reverses and neutralization of some of their top rung
activists over the years, the Khalistani terrorists still retained the capacity and substantial fire power to carry out acts of
violence.
69.       In view of these developments, the Committee feels that there is a subtle change which is taking place at the
ground level.  Therefore, there is need for being vigilant to ensure that terrorism does not rear its head once again in the
State of Punjab.  The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to take all necessary preventive measures to
thwart attempts of Pak-ISI to revive terrorism in Punjab.
70.       In this context, the Committee also draws the attention of the Government to the concern expressed by Members
regarding the plight of 400 odd policemen of Punjab facing trial in various courts for their role in anti-terrorism
operations during the heyday of terrorism in Punjab.  The trial of these policemen may have a demoralizing effect on the
policemen in general and those fighting terrorism in particular.  It becomes even more demoralizing when persons, who
spearheaded the terrorist movement from their foreign bases, are not only being allowed entry into the country but also to
move freely.  Are these recently returned separatist leaders not a threat to the security and unity of the country? 
Ironically, those who indulged in terrorism are moving freely and in sharp contrast those who fought terrorism are going
through hell of an experience.  In view of this, the Committee urges upon the Government to consider the cases of these
400 odd policemen and simultaneously cautions it to keep a strict vigil on the activities and movement of the recently
returned separatist leaders so that they do not become once again, a potent threat to the security and unity of the country.
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
LEFT WING EXTREMISM
*          The Government has been adopting two-pronged strategy of focusing on security as well as developmental aspects
of the problem.  The Coordination Centre headed by the Union Home Secretary regularly reviews and coordinates
steps taken by the affected States to check the menace of left wing extremism, monitors the plan of action in
respect of each State and makes recommendations both on development and security aspect of the problem.  The
Committee notes that the efforts of the Government are not just focused on the security aspect, the development
aspect is also receiving due attention.  In this context, the concluding remarks of the Home Secretary made by him
in his presentation before the Committee may be worthwhile to recall.  He had stated, in the context of militancy
in Jammu & Kashmir, that since many members of terrorist outfits were our own people, albeit misguided ones,
we could not think of destroying them like the USA did to the Taliban and the Al Qaeda.  Given the logic of this
guiding principle, it may be presumed that it applied in case of left wing extremists too.  Therefore, without going
into the complexities of the causes that led to the origin of left wing extremism, the Committee is of the
considered view  that the Government should make sincere efforts to engage these extremist groups in a dialogue
so as not just to identify their problems and grievances but also to find ways and means to address them.  A
process of dialogue, at this stage, appears to be a step in the right direction because each passing day will add a

new dimension to the whole problem thereby worsening the situation
further.                                                                                                                      (Para 44)
MONSTER OF COMMUNALISM
*          Communalism has been the bane of modern India.  It acted as a midwife in the partition of India and even after
that it continues to plague the social fabric of the country.  It has acquired different forms and dimensions over the
years.  However, in the recent years it is rearing its ugly head in an organized manner much in the same way as it
did in the years preceding the partition.  There are several forces which work tirelessly to ensure that it does not
lose it momentum.  These forces are the real anti-national elements who are bent upon tearing the social fabric of
the nation apart.  In their zeal to gain foothold in their respective communities, these forces are stoking communal
fire.  Their actions are spreading venom in the society which threatens to be divided along communal lines.  These
attempts to create a communal divide in the society are one of the biggest challenges before the Indian polity. 
Therefore, it needs to be nipped in the bud before it grows too large to be controlled.  It is the considered view of
this Committee that the Government must make honest and sincere efforts to maintain the pluralistic character of
the society and bring all right thinking elements of all communities together to try and find ways to check the
growing divide between them.                                      (Para 45)
                                               
POLITICISATION OF POLICE FORCES
*          In this backdrop, the Committee feels that there is need for a serious introspection by all concerned.  The
Government must act fast to stem the rot which has set in.  If immediate steps are not taken to set the house in
order, there are dangers of the system falling prey to these degenerating developments.  The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should make earnest efforts to depoliticise the institution of police before it
becomes too late to retrieve it from the morass of degeneration.  It must be ensured that police remains
accountable only to the law of the land.                                                                                                      (Para 47)
MODERNISATION OF POLICE FORCES
*          Although the Ministry of Home Affairs provides funds to the States for modernization of their police forces, the
Committee wonders what actual benefits will it accrue at the ground level?  There is all the more reason to be
apprehensive in the backdrop of total absence of a proper plan and a well thought out strategy.  Mere provision of
funds does not ensure that police forces will be modernized.  What is needed is a well chalked out plan of action
to be followed and implemented over a period of time with concrete goals in sight.  Though, a scheme is there, it
seems to be meant only for earmarking funds under a particular head as part of the annual budget making
exercise.  In view of this, the Committee is of the considered opinion that the Ministry of Home Affairs should
prepare a blueprint of a model police force to be followed by all States while drawing benefits from its scheme of
modernization of police forces.  A definite plan of action with a proper mechanism to ensure accountability is the
need of the hour.  It not only ensures accountability but also establishes unity of command and direction. 
                                             (Para 50)
REVAMP OF INTELLIGENCE APPARATUS
*          The Committee is satisfied to note the steps being taken to revamp the entire intelligence apparatus.  It hopes that
the new set-up will function smoothly.  However, with too many groups and agencies entrusted with different
aspects of intelligence, the real problem arises in regard to proper coordination amongst all of them.  The
Committee hopes that all the finer details vis-à-vis role, functions and structure of each and every functional group
and agency have been worked out so that there are least chances of overlap and conflict of functions.  In this
context, the Committee would like to lay emphasis on one more and equally important aspect of accountability. 
With so many functional units in place, there are situations when the proverbial game of passing the buck starts as
each unit points the finger towards the other to save its skin.    The Committee, therefore, is of the view that a
proper system of accountability should be evolved whereby it is easier to fix the responsibility and follow it up
with necessary action.                                             (Para52)

7.         Shri J.F. Ribeiro, in his presentation before the Committee,  submitted that the real matters of concern were cross
border terrorism, insurgency in the North-East, left wing extremism, religious fundamentalism, role of the ISI and the
nexus between drug trafficking and terrorist and insurgent groups.  While stating his views on these issues, he said that he
personally felt that terrorism finally had to be ended by the people themselves.  Another aspect on which he threw light
was that the army could not play the role of the police as it happened in Gujarat during 1985 riots which could not be
controlled by the army in five months whereas under his leadership as DGP it was controlled in a week.  He stated that
the main thing in such a situation was to deal with the persons who were fomenting the trouble.   He further stated that
fanaticism of any type should be put under control, whether it was majority fanaticism or minority fanaticism or any other
type of fanaticism.
 
7.1       Speaking on the bandhs and such type of political activity, he observed that a law was required by which the
person who called for bandhs or who called for procession or any kind of such political activity could be prosecuted.  If
the bandh turned violent then there should be a law to prosecute the persons who called for such type of activity.  He
stated that it was the police which had to face it.  To deal with it efficaciously, the police should be a professional force
and not highly politicized.   In this context, he highlighted the sufferings of the common man.   He was of the view that
what was needed now was to forget our selfishness or even our party interests and see to it that the police became
apolitical, power was not misused and that it was ensured that the police acted according to the law.  He concluded his
evidence by saying that we were still working on the fringes and the people had to help themselves otherwise their very
quality of life was being affected.
 
7.2       The Chairman and the members then sought certain clarifications from him and he was directed to send the
written replies to the queries.
 
8.         The Chairman then invited Shri Sankar Sen, to share his views on internal security situation. In his presentation
made before the Committee, Shri Sen stated that one of the biggest problems was the ineffectiveness of the police to
grapple with the internal security problems.  In this regard he cited his experience as the Director-General of National
Human Rights Commission.  The next problem according to him was the security of the tenure of the police chief which
was emphasized in the National Police Commission’s Reports and stressed upon by the National Human Rights
Commission too. He spoke about the need for operational autonomy of the police which had eroded significantly.  He
stated that in a public opinion survey, it was found that 80 per cent respondents strongly felt that political interference
with the police was a greater evil than corruption.
 
8.1       Referring to the recommendations of the National Police Commission, he said that fixation of tenure, institutional
mechanism to insulate the police as well as separation of law and order from the investigating wing were needed
forthwith.  In his view, these were the major factors responsible for the poor performance of the police. The other
problem was the inadequacy of training.  Citing his experience during his association with National Police
Academy(NPA) and later with BPR&D, he stated that there were no proper training institutions except NPA nor were
there any quality trainers.  He suggested for the structural changes which were also strongly recommended by the
National Police Commission. 
 
8.2       Another important point which he mentioned was the increasing lawlessness and escalating crime.  He later
referred to the percentage of the crimes registered.  Regarding organized crimes, he stated that an agency was required at
the national level to tackle this menace.  He said that during his tenure with the BSF, he felt the need for curbing the
illegal immigration which had the capacity of changing the demographic profile of some of the bordering districts.
According to him the scenario had dangerous portents.  The other aspect on which he drew the attention of the Committee
was the requisitioning of the army to deal with any law and order situation at the drop of the hat.  He touched upon 
several reasons responsible for the internal disturbances and the deteriorating law and order situation. The working of the
prosecutions, he believed, was also required to be thought over seriously. He suggested for a law to ensure greater
coordination between the prosecution and the police.  Lastly, while referring to the  Maharashtra  Control of Organised
Crime Act,  he emphasized the need for a special law to deal with the organized crime.
