National Academy of Administration in catering to the training needs of services other than the IAS, desires that
the Academy should devise short-term in-house departmental capsule courses for the new entrant officers in
respective departments on a quarterly basis. Attending these courses for all newly posted officers from the level of
Under Secretary and above should be made mandatory. Similar quarterly capsule courses should be devised for
new entrants below rank of Under Secretary to impart complete knowledge about the Department. The course
content of the LBSNAA for the junior civil servants should include subjects like agriculture. By incorporating the
detailed knowledge of various Departments to the Departmental training programmes, the LBSNAA could increase
the time in the inputs for improving the Agricultural contents in the probationers
course.                                                                           (Para 23)
l The Committee taking note of the declining seriousness of the participants in the training programmes, feel that this
decline is perhaps more due to the lack of relevance to the actual job and as such the course contents should be
made relevant to his/her posting. Further, the training programmes for junior level officers should include
components on self-awareness and human values and inputs that would enable them to improve their basic attitude
and have a better understanding of ground level conditions. The Committee opines that such training programme
should include awareness of the Freedom of Information Act, 2002 for bringing in transparency in the
administrative functions of the
Government.                                                                                                                                 (Para 25)
l While appreciating the efforts of the Academy to imbibe ethics and positive values in the participants, the
Committee recommends that such training should be broad based to cater to maximum number of officers. It is of
the opinion that training programmes need to impart skills for interaction with the public in a humane manner.
(Para 27)
l The Committee feels that one of the major reasons for lack of interest especially in the foundation and probationary
courses, is the complacency the trainees have developed that all of them will inevitably be declared as passed.
Trainees who fail in various subjects are allowed to reappear at the next examination and the next and so on till
eventually they are declared as pass. The confirmation of services of those who fail in various subjects makes a
mockery of the word “probationer”. There is urgent need for Government to review their policy regarding
probationers who fail in subjects prescribed in the course. The Committee is of the view that probationers who fails
to clear all the examinations set out for them should be declared as failed and then services terminated. Only in
proven cases where a probationer fails for reasons beyond his control should he be permitted to appear just once
more and if he fails again termination of his service should be the rule.                                                   (Para
27.1)SELECTION BOARD
l The Committee is not happy with the high vacancy position in PSUs for want of recommendations of PESB. It
urges upon the PESB to expedite its recommendations in the pending cases so that delays do not take place in
filling up the board level vacancies in PSUs.                                                                               (Para 29.0)
l The Committee expresses its concern at the evidently slow pace in which DOPT is taking action on the cases
cleared by PESB. The Committee recommends that the DOPT should pursue the recommendations of PESB
pending with the Ministries/Departments and work out ways to fill up the vacancies in a time bound manner. (Para
29.1)
        MODERNISATION OF GOVERNMENT OFFICES
l The Committee is of the view that modernizing the entire administrative apparatus should not be an end in itself.
There should be an attitudinal change in the civil servants to serve the public at large. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Government should work out ways to imbibe attitudinal change in its personnel for better
delivery of services to the public.                                                                                                                 (Para 31)
l The Committee also urges upon the Government to evolve clearly measurable parameters to assess the degree of

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
improvement made and also monitor those parameters on an effectively periodic basis.
                                                                                                                               (Para 31.1)
        NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF SMART GOVERNMENT
l The Committee views that delay in execution of plan schemes defeat the purpose of the scheme. It, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should follow up its proposal with the Cabinet and Planning Commission and make
the National Institute of Smart Government (NISG) functional.
        (Para 33)
        GOOD GOVERNANCE
l The Committee is of the view that with the help of e-governance, computers, improvement of information
technology, Freedom of Information and Citizens' Charters, collection of basic data and information available with
the Ministry will show a marked improvement if they are constantly updated. The Committee hopes that not only
statistical information but the parameters of decision making also should in due course be made available to the
people.   (Para 35)
        RIGHTSIZING OF THE GOVERNMENT
l While appreciating the Government’s policy of rightsizing and rationalizing of the Government machinery, it is of
the opinion that the functions, activities and administrative structure of each Ministry/Department should be clearly
chalked out so that overlapping between them do not take place. A review of the Ministries/Departments not
covered by the Expenditure Reforms Commission may be made with a view to rightsizing and rationalising them. It
will be highly desirable to carry out a manpower audit of each Department. Blanket abolition of certain percentage
of posts can on the one hand cripple the functioning of one Department and another Department warranting even
greater reduction will escape. A meaningful manpower audit of each Department alone can make this exercise truly
rational.        (Para 37)
l The Committee, therefore, recommends that downsizing should be followed up vigorously in its pursuit to improve
administrative efficiency and effectiveness.                                                                  (Para 38)
l The Committee is of the view that the Government cannot downsize its personnel meaningfully without enlisting
the support of major political parties. Therefore, the Government should hold all party meeting to arrive at a
consensus to execute the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission which recommended the downsizing of
Government while recommending greatly enhanced pay scales. This is a matter of national interest and we cannot
afford to delay it indefinitely. The result of manpower audits will be really helpful in getting the required
consensus.    (Para 40)
        CITIZEN’S CHARTER
l While taking note of the number of Citizen’s Charters brought out by Central Government Ministries/Departments
and States/UTs, the Committee recommends that the Government should vigorously pursue with the concerned
Ministries/Department and States/UTs who have not brought out their Citizen’s Charters. Copies of Citizen’s
Charters framed by Ministries/Departments need to be given to all Members of Parliament as and when they are
prepared to elicit their suggestions for effective improvements in governance.                                 (Para 42)
        INFORMATION & FACILITATION COUNTERS
l While taking note of the information furnished by the Ministry with regard to the setting up of IFCs, the Committee
reiterates its earlier view that the Government should monitor each of the Ministries/Departments/organizations
who have not set up their IFCs and render necessary assistance thereto and submit a detailed report of its
monitoring to the Committee in its ATR.                                                                                                             
(Para 44)
        PUBLIC GRIEVANCE REDRESSAL
l The Committee feels that there is need for publicity (India wide) through Doordarshan to enable the rural folk to
know about the existence of these two channels for the redressal of public grievances. Secondly in some cases the
replies received by the aggrieved do not provide solace and redressal expected from the grievance redressal
mechanism of the Government. The output, it is felt cannot reach the desired level without putting an effective
Department-wise monitoring mechanism that studies the measurable parameters which show tangible results.          
(Para 46)
l The Committee, while taking note of the above measures to strengthen the grievance mechanism, recommends that

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
all out efforts should be made to effectively monitor the same and due attention should be given to timely redressal
of grievances lodged. It is also of the considered view that officers responsible for brooking delay should be made
accountable and suitable action taken against them. This mechanism may bring some success to computer savvy
public, but the bulk of India lives in villages. It is therefore that stress has been laid for evolving a mechanism that
would serve the less literates. The Committee expresses a desire to see the results of one such monitoring of each
Department.                                                                                                                                 (Para 48)
        DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS' WELFARE
l The Committee notes the attempts made by the Ministry for revision of pension/family pension of Government
employees. The Committee recommends that the Department should set out  specific time frames for various
categories of grievances, and obtain from all Departments an annual return to assess the efficacy of grievance
redressal adopted by various Departments. It is hoped that a summary of such Department-wise analysis shall be
made in the Annual Reports of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions in all future years.               
(Para 50)
        CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
l The reply of the Government in tackling the issue of vacancies reflects that the observations/recommendations of
the Committee contained in its 87th Report for initiating the selection process well in advance of the occurrence of
the vacancies has not been heeded by the Government thereby delaying the filling up of such vacancies. The
Committee, while taking serious not would like to know the action taken by Government against the officers who
failed to comply with Government Orders for initiating the process of filling up prospective vacancies.   (Para 52)
l It has come to notice of the Committee that when CAT gives a judgement in the case of one serving officer e.g. in
fixing the seniority of State Service Officer when they are promoted to the IAS or IPS or regarding adding the army
service towards the seniority of an ex-army officer, the relief remains limited to the officers that approached CAT,
and that the Government do not extend the same relief suo-moto to other officers placed in identical situation. As a
result every individual officer has to spend time and money to approach CAT individually before he can get the
same relief granted in the first case. This policy multiplies the number of litigants on the one hand, and on the other
hand erodes the faith of officers in the Government about its intrinsic will to give justice to them and tells on their
morale. The policy has been followed since several decades. The Committee feels that it militates against the
concept of natural justice and it would like the Government to inform the Committee why a principle decided by
CAT or the Higher Courts should not be extended ipso-facto and suo-moto to all officers placed in identical
circumstances.   (Para 52.1)
l The Committee notes the 9% decrease in number of cases at the end of 2002. However, considering the large
number of brought forward cases, it desires that the Government should classify cases age-wise and give priority in
clearing pendency of cases age-wise. It should also undertake a study to be completed in a specific time-frame to
identify the cases that have caused this huge accumulation and then take effective steps to eradicate those cases.
The Committee however records its satisfaction that the number of cases disposed of has exceeded the number of
cases instituted in all the years after 1999 with a considerable margin.                                                         (Para 54)
l The Committee records its appreciation of the steps taken by the Government in marshalling the contribution of the
National Council (JCM) and BOA in the disposal of cases relating to employees of the Government. The
Committee desires that Government should undertake a quarterly review of cases brought before the National
Council to expedite the pendency.                                                                                                            (Para 56)
l The Committee would like to know the reasons of the respective four States for seeking the abolition of the
Tribunals, as well as the Government’s considered views regarding those reasons. It may be desirable for the
Government to share with the Committee the nature of amendments the Government is proposing to make in the
Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985. In all events the Committee desires that this entire exercise should be carried
out with a high degree of urgency.
(Para 58)
        CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
l The Committee takes serious note of the high pendency of cases for implementation of advice of the CVC in the
Ministries/Departments. In administration the objective of rewards and punishment gets completely defeated unless
they are awarded with utmost promptness. This is specially true about punishments. As promptness in punishments

99th report of Committee on HOME AFFAIRS
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/99threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:58:50]
has a salutary effect on the tone of administration and in the light of the fact that the CVC is directly responsible to
the Parliament, there appears no escape for the Committee but to directly involve itself through an in-depth study of
the problem of delays of more than six months in thousands of cases. The Ministry has enumerated six reasons for
the delays. The Committee therefore would like to have break up of all the delayed cases of the past five years that
are respectively attributable to the six stated reasons in para 59.2. It would further like to know the specific
remedial measures that Government intends to adopt to tackle each of the six categories of reasons respectively.
Additionally, the Committee would like to know how the Government intend to implement each of the measures it
so suggests for example, in the measures already suggested by the Government in Para 59.3; how exactly will it be
possible to implement the measures given at (a) & (b) in Para 59.3. Further, in what way are the delays going to be
reduced by resorting to action proposed in (c), (d) & (e) of Para 59.3 ? Of the measures contemplated to curb
delays, barring (a) of Para 59.3, none of the other measures contemplated seem to have any direct bearing on the
‘causes of delay’ as enumerated in clauses (a), (c), (d), (e) & (f) of Para 59.2. That being the case, the Committee
has grave doubts if the measures contemplated will at all make any dent on the problem of delays.              (Para
60.0)
l Till an in-depth study is made by the Committee to effectively deal with this problem in a systematic and sustained
basis, the Committee has the following to suggest:
        As each case of punishment has its own unique complexities, it is therefore suggested that in the light of the
complexities of each case which would be apparent to the CVC before it tenders the first stage advise, the CVC
must prescribe specific time frames with dates by which Ministries/Departments/Organisations must report to the
CVC about the implementation of CVC’s first stage advice. The same should be done in respect of the second stage
advice. If the Ministries/Departments/Organisations find that the time frame prescribed by the CVC is impractical,
they themselves must inform the CVC within seven days of the receipt of the advice as to the date by which they
shall be able to report the said implementation. If, thus the Ministries/Departments/Organisations fail to keep up to
their own suggested dates, the CVC should report to the head of the Department for taking action against the
dealing officer for inability to abide by his own date. Initially, warnings to such officers should be placed on their
personal files but if his performance does not improve even after three warnings, major punishment proceedings
should be initiated against that officer for incompetent handling of his duties. The Committee believes that the root
of the problem of delays lies in the absence of accountability of the dealing officers of the CVC, and the dealing
officers of the Ministries/Departments/Organisations and it is here where the action should commence
forthwith.                                      (Para 60.1)
l     In the Meanwhile, the Committee, in consultation with the Ministry and the CVC shall in due course evolve a
permanent operational procedure.                                                                                            (Para 60.2)
        SCHEME FOR COMPASSIONATE APPOINTMENT
l The responses of the Ministry to the afore-mentioned questions are not satisfactory. The committee feels that the
matter of compassionate appointments requires detailed discussion to formulate its
views/suggestions/recommendations. The Committee, therefore, requests the Ministry to furnish clear-cut answers
to the afore-mentioned questions within six weeks time from the date of presentation of its Report to Parliament to

subject.                                                                                                                              (Para 62.1)

The different Central Para -military Forces namely. BSF. ITBP . CRPF, Assam Rifles and•CISF 
have been raised for different purpose s. Border Security Force (DSF) is primarily meant for 
border deployment to check infiltration, trans-border crimes on the Indo-Pakistan and Indo ·

has been raised to assist States/UTs in interna l security duties. Assam Rifles (A R) is meant for 
providing security of North-Eastern sector and the international border and carry out counter­
insurgency operations in North-Eastern States. Central Indust rial Security Force (ClSF) bas been 
raised for the protection and security of industrial undertakings owned by the Central

Rapid Action Force has been raised to deal with situations arising out of communal tenstons 
including riots and not-like situations. The Force has a composite character representing various 
sections of the society. Personnel are selected from the CRPF after careful screening and special 
training is imparted to them including traming in riot control, relief and rescue operations. fir~ 
•t1.htmg and first-aid. lt was decided to convert 10 CRPF Battalions into 16 Battalions of RAl' 
ureters constituting this Force were issued in December, 91 and the force became operatiOnal 
w.e.f. 7.10.92. Each RAF Battalion is divided into 4 teams and each team had separate elements 
lor riot-control/ tear-smoke and firing. The Force also specially equipped to deal with riots and 
special weapons/equipmo:nts provided lo the Force include riot a.s guns, shock sticks, fibre glaS5 
helmets poly-carbonte lathis/shields, etc. Additional vehicles were also provided to facilitate very 
qutck response. The Force had been raised by convening unattached CRPF Bns. into RAF Bns. 
The Standard cost of raising an unattached CRPF Bn. is approximately Rs. 15.50 crores. An 
additional expenditure of Rs. 1.50 erores is required to convert an unattached CRPF Bn into a 
RAF Bn., to meet the cost of additional manpower and equipments. The annual maintenance of 
a RAF Bn. is approx. Rs.S crores. The RAF battalion is part of the CRPF and hence no separate 
budget is provided to the RAF. Present strength of RAF consisted of 5 battalions. It was 
proposed to convert 5 more CRPF battalions to RAF.

present this One hundredth Report on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) relating to the Department
of Development of North Eastern Region.

REPORT
The North Eastern Region comprises of 8 States of Arunchal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim. Excluding Sikkim, the region covers an area
of 255,000 sq. kms representing around 7.8 per cent of the total area of the country. It is a
distinct geographical entity connected with the rest of the country through a narrow corridor in
North Bengal thereby standing out as a classic example of cultural and geographical isolation from
the other composite States of India. The region shares 98 per cent of its borders with other South
East Asian countries viz. Bhutan and China in the North, Myanmar in the East and Bangladesh in
the South and West.
1.2 The region has a total population of 38.5 million as per 2001 census which is around 3.75
per cent of the country’s population.
1.3 The North Eastern States are categorised as Special Category States which entitles them to
receive 90% of the Central plan assistance as grants. However funds are not allocated State-wise.
Instead, Project specific assistance is released for sanctioned projects under the Central Pool. The
release of funds to the State Governments depends on their capacity to formulate sound project
proposals, utilize the funds released and the pace of implementation of the projects on the ground.
These funding sources and quantum of funds broadly take care of the requirement for development
programmes of the North Eastern States and are intended to continue till the Region reaches a
certain minimum level in terms of infrastructure development.
2. The Department of Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) was constituted in
September, 2001. An extract of the amendments to the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961 containing the work allocation to the Department is as follows:
• Matters related to the planning, execution and monitoring of developmental schemes
and projects of North Eastern region including those in the sectors of power, irrigation,
roads and communications.
• Hill Areas Development Programme and Border Areas Development Programme in
North Eastern region.
• Non-lapsable fund for the North Eastern region.
• North Eastern Council.
• North Eastern Development Finance Institution (NEDFI).
• North Eastern Regional Agricultural Marketing Corporation Limited (NERAMAC).
• Sikkim Mining Corporation Limited (SMC).
• North Eastern Handlooms and Handicrafts Development Corporation (NEHHDC).
• Road works financed in whole or in part by the Central Government in the North
Eastern region.
• Planning of road and inland waterways transport in the North Eastern region.
3. The thrust of the Department in the development of North Eastern region consists of
improving infrastructure, providing greater access to basic social services like education, health,
drinking water and sanitation, etc., expanding economic and social opportunities for all, building

2
capacities aimed at increased efficiency, creating an environment for private participation conducive
to growth, and providing a policy frame to influence in a positive manner, wide ranging economic
activities having employment/income generation potential.

NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
15. The North-Eastern Council was set up in 1972, following the enactment of the North
Eastern Council Act, 1971. For a long time, the North Eastern States had been demanding
restructuring of the Council so as to make it more effective. In pursuance of the demand, the
North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002 came into force on 23rd December, 2002. In terms
of the amendment, Sikkim has become the eighth member of the Council. The composition of the
Council has been revised and now consists of the Governors and Chief Ministers of Arunachal
Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tripura. In addition, three
members are to be nominated by the President of India to the Council. The President of India may,
if deemed necessary, nominate a Union Minister to be a member of the Council. The Chairman of
the Council will be nominated by the President. By practice, the Governor of one of the
Member States is nominated as Chairman. Presently, the Governor of Assam is the Chairman of
the Council.
15.1 The Council’s functions have also been modified and it is now to function as a regional
planning body for the North-Eastern region. While formulating the regional plan, the Council will
give priority to schemes and projects which benefit two or more States, with the exception of
Sikkim for which the Council will formulate State-specific Projects and Schemes. The Council will
also review, from time to time, implementation of projects and schemes, progress of expenditure
and measures taken by the Member States for the maintenance of security and public order and
recommend to the State Governments further measures to be taken in this regard. For
accomplishing the above functions, the Council shall have such powers as may be delegated to it
by the Central Government. In terms of the amendment, the Council is required to meet at least
twice a year. The amendment also provides for participation of a representative of Department of
Development of North Eastern Region in the meetings of the Council.

NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES FOR DEVELOPMENT OF NORTH
EASTERN REGION (NLCPR)
20. The Non-Lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) has been constituted out of the
unspent amount from 10% of the budget of various Union Ministries and Departments (except
those specifically exempted) exclusively earmarked for the socio-economic development of the
North East. Budget for the purpose is defined as Gross Budgetary Support to the Plan, which is
inclusive of Externally Aided Projects.
20.1 Until recently, the Planning Commission was handling the Non-lapsable Central Pool of
Resources (NLCPR). The work has since been transferred to DoNER. The broad objective of this
pool is to ensure speedy development of the socio-economic infrastructure in North Eastern region
by increasing the flow of budgetary financing for new infrastructure/projects/schemes in the
region. Both physical and social infrastructure sectors such as irrigation and flood control, power,
roads and bridges, education, health, water supply and sanitation—are considered for providing
support under the Central Pool with projects in physical infrastructure sector receiving priority.
Only project specific assistance is released from the NLCPR and no diversion is permissible.

8
20.2 Funds from the NLCPR can be released for State sector as well as Central sector projects/
schemes. However, the available funds are not meant to supplement the normal plan programmes
either of the State Governments or of the Union Ministries/Departments/Agencies.

North Eastern Development Finance Institution (NEDFI)
24.1 NEDFI was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 on 9 August, 1995 with its
registered office at Guwahati. The main objectives of NEDFI are to carry on and transact the
business of providing credit and other facilities for promotion, expansion and modernisation of
industrial enterprises and infrastructure projects in the North Eastern region and also to carry on
and transact the business of providing credit and other facilities for promotion of agri-horticulture/
medicinal/sericulture plantations, aquaculture, poultry, dairy and animal husbandry development in
order to initiate large involvement of the rural population in the economic upsurge of the society
and faster economic growth of different parts of the North Eastern region.
24.2 NEDFI is a Public Financial Institution under Section 4 A of the Companies Act, 1956. It

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
The Non-lapsable Central Pool of Resources (NLCPR) became operational in April,
1998. The pool has come into existence out of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure
norm of 10% by each Central Ministry/Department for the North-Eastern region. The total
amount accrued to this pool during 1998-2002 was Rs.5806.07 crore. Thus, on an average a
little over Rs.1400 crore accrued to NLCPR. Consequent upon the exercise undertaken by
DoNER to ascertain the actual size of the pool, Rs.2853.97 crore were calculated to be
available in it as on 1 April, 2002, after taking into account the debits. However, only
Rs.1318.66 crore have been released to the States during 1998-2002. The release of
Rs.1318.66 crore during 1998-2002 is less than 50% of the cost of the sanctioned projects
worth Rs.2728 crore. (Para 25)
As on date, a total of 548 projects have been sanctioned out of NLCPR with an
approved cost of Rs.3097.24 crore. In sharp contrast to that only Rs.1868.66 crore have
actually been released leaving a committed liability of Rs.1228.58 crore. Against this
requirement, a provision of only Rs.550 crore has been made in BE 2003-04. (Para 25.1)
The above figures clearly indicate that the amount being released out of this central
pool of resources is far less than the accruals to it. There are two aspects of the mechanism
evolved to ensure adequate flow of funds to the process of socio-economic development in
the North-Eastern region. One, Central Ministries/Departments (except for a few exempted)
are required to earmark 10% of their gross budgetary support exclusively for North-Eastern
region. However, statistics prove that Central Ministries/Departments have only been, able
to spend in the range of 6 to 7% out of the earmarked 10% of their gross budgetary
support. (Para 25.2)
The second aspect flows from the first one. The inability of the Central Ministries/
Departments to spend the whole of the 10%, paved the way for creation of NLCPR which
is, as stated elsewhere, constituted of the shortfalls in the stipulated expenditure norm of
10%. As stated in the preceding paragraphs, the release of funds out of this pool is less
than 50% of its actual size. (Para 25.2.1)
After having had a look at the two aspects of the mechanism evolved to ensure flow
of funds, it becomes amply clear that neither 10% norm nor NLCPR has been able to
maintain a steady flow of funds. Although, on an average Rs.1400 crore accrue to this pool
every year, the annual release out of it has hovered around Rs.300 crore or so. This proves
that there is a clear mismatch between the accruals and the release of funds. As against
a projected requirement of Rs.1050 crore for 2003-04, the Planning Commission has
approved only Rs.550 crore. The amount sanctioned by Planning Commission is on the lower
side keeping in view the fact that Sikkim has also become part of the North-Eastern region.
In this way, the purpose behind setting up of NLCPR is getting defeated as adequate funds
are not flowing out of it. (Para 25.3)
25.4 In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Government should not
only release the backlog amount of Rs.1228.58 crore out of NLCPR to enable the DoNER
13

14
to maintain the momentum of developmental activities in the North-Eastern region but it
should also ensure pro rata release of funds out of total accruals to NLCPR henceforth.
NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL (NEC)
During Ninth Five Y ear Plan, an outlay of Rs. 2114 crore was made for NEC. Out of
that Rs.1970.90 crore were allocated to it and Rs.1937.71 crore were actually spent by
it. The annual allocation during the plan period progressively grew from Rs.324 crore in
1997-98 to Rs. 450 crore in the terminal year i.e. 2001-02. Similarly, during the Tenth Plan,
the Planning Commission has made an outlay of Rs.3500 crore for NEC. Out of this
plan outlay, Rs.450 crore were allocated for 2002-03 which has now been enhanced to
Rs.500 crore.
Thus, the pattern of allocations to NEC followed during the Ninth Plan is being
adhered to in the Tenth Plan also. In other words, the flow of funds to NEC continues to
be progressive in nature starting with lower allocation in the first year and then gradually
going up with the progression of the Plan. In contrast to NEC’s projection of Rs. 800 crore
for 2003-04, only Rs. 500 crore have been provided to it and that too when Sikkim has
recently joined as the eighth member of the Council.
Here, the Committee would like to emphasise the point that annual allocations out
of plan outlay should be on the higher side in the initial years of the plan period so that
the projected activities get underway with a head start. The Committee is of the view that
the maximum momentum should be provided in the beginning of the Plan so that its steady
progression is maintained in later years also. Besides, as a Plan progresses, the value of the
allocations in real terms declines with the passage of time. Therefore, by providing a
sizeable chunk of the outlay in the first two years of the Plan, an optimum use of the funds
can be made. In this background, the Committee is of the view that the Government should
enhance NEC’s allocation as per actual requirements projected by it.
In addition, the Government may also consider to place the unutilised funds of the
NLCPR at the disposal of the North-Eastern Council. (Para 26, 26.1, 26.2 and 26.3)
The North-Eastern Council has recently been remodelled as a regional planning body
with its emphasis on projects and schemes involving two or more States. Over the years,
NEC has, primarily, been playing the role of a central funding agency. As a result, it has
not been able to focus its attention on a balanced regional growth. In the absence of a
comprehensive planning for the region aimed at all-round development, the North-Eastern
region continues to lag behind. The Committee, therefore, is of the considered view that the
North-Eastern Council should play a proactive role in the development of the North-Eastern
region while focusing its attention on regional planning. (Para 27)
VRS PACKAGE FOR SIKKIM MINING CORPORATION
28. Sikkim Mining Corporation has been incurring losses ever since it came into
existence. Efforts to revive it by way of providing budgetary grants and loans have proved
futile. As a result of that the burden of losses, interests, salaries, etc. continues to mount.
With a view to bring about a turnaround in the ailing PSU, a restructuring plan was
submitted by DoNER to the Planning Commission which has since been rejected by it. After
the rejection of restructuring plan, there is another proposal which seeks to rationalise the
manpower of the corporation by offering ‘Voluntary Retirement Scheme’ package which
entails an expenditure of Rs.2.5 crore. The implementation of this VRS package is expected
to reduce the burden of salaries to the employees to a great extent which, in turn, will help

15
in putting the loss making PSU back on track. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
the VRS package for the employees of Sikkim Mining Corporation should be put through
at the earliest. (Para 28)
IMPROVEMENT IN ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE
Roads are an important engine of growth. For a region as remote as the North-East,
the development of a good network of roads is a sine qua non for an all-round socio-
economic development. There is an urgent need to take necessary steps to bring about
qualitative and visible improvement in the condition of roads. For, poor condition of roads
will prove to be a big hurdle in attracting private investment in various sectors. Therefore,
keeping in view the crucial importance of a good road network, the Committee recommends
that a comprehensive action plan should be formulated by the Government to improve,
expand and maintain a durable and reliable road network in the North-Eastern region.
(Para 29)
TECHNOLOGY MISSIONS
30. North-Eastern region is full of natural resources such as medicinal plants, bamboo,
horticulture, floriculture, agricultural products such as ginger and potato, etc. These natural
products have a potential to catapult the region to the position of being a major base for
agri-business and agri-exports. Another bountiful natural resource is water which can be
harnessed in a big way to generate hydel-electricity. The hydel-electricity potential of the
region is 32000 MW which, if realised optimally, can transform the region as the
powerhouse of the country. Similarly, oil and natural gas is also a major potential area
which could prove to be a big help in import substitution.
30.1. Undoubtedly, the North-Eastern region is a resource-rich area. But the abundant
resources of the region have remained untapped. Consequently, it has lagged behind in the
national process of development. Today, the region is beset with multiple problems such as
unemployment, economic backwardness, low industrial development, poor social and
economic infrastructure etc. In order to overcome these problems, concerted, well-
coordinated, focused and persistent efforts are needed.
30.2 The Committee, therefore, is of the considered opinion that the Government should
launch ‘Technology Missions’ with a view to harness the immense potential of various areas
within a fixed time-frame. (Para 30, 30.1 and 30.2)
PROMOTION OF TOURISM
31. North-Eastern States are not rich just in natural resources but they are also endowed
with pristine natural beauty. This virgin beauty has, however, remained beyond the reach
of people from other parts of the country as well as foreigners due to a variety of reasons
such as poor tourist infrastructure, lack of adequate rail and air services, less exposure to
the outside world, spread of insurgency-related violence in various parts, etc. All these and
many other factors have contributed to the non-realisation of the potential of the tourism
sector.
31.1 As the times are changing and the region is now getting more and more exposed
coupled with a strong urge among the people to attain economic prosperity and self-
sufficiency, the time is opportune to showcase the region as a major tourist destination.
Therefore, the Committee is of the view that a comprehensive plan should be prepared and
implemented to give the much-needed boost to the tourism industry in the North-Eastern
region. The Committee hopes that such a step will prove to be a major turning point in the
economic development of the region. (Para 31 and 31.1)

4. Budget Estimates of Election Commission for the year 2003-2004 includes the budgetary
allocation of Delimitation Commission. The parameters for the working of the Delimitation
Commission are contained in the Delimitation Act, 2002 and have also been detailed in the guidelines
framed by the Commission. Pursuant to the enactment of the Constitution (Eighty-fourth
Amendment) Act, 2001, the Delimitation Act, 2002 was enacted. The Delimitation Commission is
a three member body constituted on 12.7.2002, under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002

3
with Shri Justice Kuldip Singh, a retired Judge of the Supreme Court, as its Chairperson and
Shri B.B. Tandon, one of the Election Commissioners and the third Member of the Commission is
the Election Commissioner of the concerned State that is being delimited. The main task of the
Commission is to readjust the division of territorial constituencies of the seats in the House of the
People allocated to each State and the readjustment of the division of territorial constituencies of
the total number of seats in the Legislative Assembly of each State. The rationalisation of the
constituencies shall be on the basis of the 1991 census figures. The Commission will also refix
the seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes on the basis of that census.
The Commission has started functioning with the secretarial assistance from the Election
Commission of India and is expected to complete its work within two years.
4.1 When asked about the guidelines for the Associate Members of the Commission, the
Government in its written reply stated that under the provisions of the Delimitation Act, 2002, the
Commission is required to delimit the Assembly and Parliamentary Constituencies in respect of all
States (excepting Jammu and Kashmir) and the UT of Pondicherry and NCT of Delhi. As per
guidelines the Commission prepares Paper-1 and Paper-2 in respect of each State relating to
distribution of total assembly seats among various districts and entitlement of the seats to be
reserved for Scheduled Castes to various districts respectively in each State. These papers are yet
to be prepared in respect of Assam, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Manipur, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh and West
Bengal where the data of 1991 census prepared and submitted by the Chief Electoral Officers is
being checked for correctness in the Commission.
4.2 The Working Papers (which includes Paper-l and Paper-2) containing detailed proposals
have already been prepared and discussed with the Associate Members from the States of Goa,
Mizoram, Rajasthan and Sikkim. They have been asked to send their dissenting notes and after
receiving their dissenting notes, if any, draft proposals will be published in the State and Central
Gazettes inviting objections and suggestions from the public.
4.3 In respect of the States of Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh,
Haryana, Punjab, Madhya Pradesh and NCT of Delhi, Papers-l and 2 have been sent to the
Associate members who are requested to attend meetings fixed during the period of 1st April to
17th April, 2003. The Members have been requested to give their proposals in writing at the
respective meetings so as to enable the Commission to prepare Working Papers with full proposals
on the basis of the suggestions made by them.
4.4 Out of the eleven remaining States, fresh nomination of 5 MLAs each as Associate Members
from the States of Himachal Pradesh, Tripura, Nagaland and Meghalaya after the formation of new
Legislative Assemblies in February, 2003 are awaited. As soon as the Associate Members are
nominated by the Hon’ble Speakers of the respective Legislative Assemblies, Paper-l and 2 relating
to these States will be sent to the Associate members calling them for meetings.
4.5 For the remaining seven States of Bihar , Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Pondicherry, Tamil
Nadu and Uttaranchal, Papers-l and 2 are ready, and the dates for first meetings will be fixed in
due course.
4.6 When asked about adoption of 1971 procedure instead of framing new procedure, the
Department in its written reply stated that in substance the procedure followed by the Commission
is by and large the same as followed by the 1971 Commission. The Minister of Law and Justice
sent a letter to the Commission on 17 March, 2003 conveying general feeling at the all political
parties’ meeting held on March 13, 2003 regarding consultation with Associate Members in the
process of formulation of draft delimitation proposals. In deference to the general feeling expressed
at the said meeting, the Commission have decided to adopt the revised Guidelines for the
delimitation of constituencies under the Delimitation Act, 2002.

4
4.7 The Delimitation Commission has always felt that due regard and respect have to be given
to the views of the Associate Members while carrying out the delimitation exercise and has
endeavoured to do this. However, since it has been brought to the notice of the Delimitation
Commission that there is some dissatisfaction amongst Associate Members on the methodology that
has been adopted by the Commission while carrying out its functions, the Delimitation Commission
has written back to the Minister for Law and Justice saying that from now onwards the Associate

paper is finalised indicating the proposed allocation of assembly seats to various districts in the

DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
6.0 This Department has a two-tier organisational set up i.e. the Main Secretariat at New Delhi
and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore.
6.1 The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are:
(i) to extend advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India

(ii) to carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government;

(iv) to deal with the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil Laws;
(v) to authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of
the President under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution;
(vi) to appoint law officers such as Attorney General of India, Solicitor General of India
and the Additional Solicitors-General of India and
(vii) to sanction grants-in-aid to certain institutions engaged in research in the field of law,
constitutional studies and Parliamentary institutions.

Act, 1961, the Notaries Act, 1952 and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. The Department
is also administratively in-charge of the Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange (ATFE), Income

AFFAIRS
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
7.0 The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs in his deposition before the Committee stated
that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal which decides appeals against the orders of the
Departmental authorities in respect of all direct taxes, has a pendency of 1,82,625 cases at the end
of February, 2003. Number of measures have been adopted to reduce pendency of cases such as
clubbing of cases having similar issues, identification of small cases for quick disposal,
identification of cases involving issues already covered by the decisions of the Supreme Court,
raising the limit from Rs.l lakh to Rs.5 lakh for appeals to be heard by a single Member, formation
of mobile Benches etc. As a result of these measures the increase in pendency has been arrested
and it is going down. Most of the Benches of ITAT are housed in private accommodation taken
on rent. There is also a problem of providing suitable residential accommodation to Members of
ITAT. On these aspects a public interest litigation is pending in the Supreme Court and the Supreme
Court has been issuing directions from time to time regarding providing office accommodation as
well as accommodation for residential purposes for the Members of ITAT. The Department has
been trying to meet the directions of the Supreme Court within the available financial resources and
there is a genuine need to construct office accommodation for various Benches of ITAT as also
to provide residential accommodation to Members of ITAT. The Department sought the support of
the this Committee for the construction of infrastructure for the Tribunal so as to ensure smooth
and efficient discharge of its functions.
7.1 The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of
including the financial proposals for the requirement of accommodation for official as well as
residential purposes for the ITAT under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the Development
of Infrastructural Facilities for the Judiciary through hundred per cent central funding.
National Legal Services Authority
8.0 The Secretary in his deposition before the Committee stated that the National Legal Services
Authority is engaged in providing legal services, legal aid and speedy justice through Lok Adalats.

8
The Authority having its office at New Delhi is headed by the Chief Justice of India who is the
ex-officio  Patron-in-Chief. Similarly, State Legal Services Authorities and District Legal Services
Authorities have been constituted in every State. Supreme Court Legal Services Committee, High
Court Legal Services Committees and Taluk Legal Services Committees have also been constituted
in every State. As per the information available with NALSA, as on 31 December, 2002 about
47.43 lakh persons have benefited through court-oriented legal aid programmes. Till date about
1 lakh 55 thousand Lok Adalats have been organised wherein about 1 crore 46 lakhs cases have
been settled. It was felt that a major drawback in the existing scheme of organisation of Lok
Adalats under Chapter VI of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was that the system of Lok
Adalats was mainly based on conciliation/compromise or settlement between the parties. If the
parties do not arrive at any compromise or settlement, the case is either returned to the court of
law or the parties are advised to seek remedy in a court of law. The Legal Services Authorities
Act, 1987, was, therefore, amended in 1995 and provisions for Pre-Litigation Conciliation and
Settlement have been inserted in the Act. With this amendment, Lok Adalats have been given power
to decide the cases involving public utility services like transport service, posts, telephones,
electricity, sanitation, hospitals, insurance services, etc., involving an amount of not more than
Rs. 10 lakh, on merits, in case the parties fail to arrive at any compromise or settlement. The cases
involving these public utility services need to be settled urgently. So most of the cases which ought
not to go in the regular courts would be settled at pre-litigation stage itself which would result in
reducing the work load of the regular courts to a great extent.
8.1 The Committee appreciates the establishment of permanent Lok Adalats which would
go a long way in bringing down the pendency of cases before the courts.
Law Commission
9.0 The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body constituted by the Government once
in three years. The Commission was originally constituted in 1955. The present 16th Law
Commission was constituted on 1 September, 2000. It consists of a  Chairman, three full-time
Members, one Member-Secretary and three or more Part-Time Members depending upon the nature
of work. At present, besides the Chairman and the Member-Secretary, one Full-Time Member are
in position. The Law Commission has submitted 185 Reports ( Annexure-I).
9.1 Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary source of law for Parliament as well
as judiciary. Law Commission present its Report to the Government, the Government then lay those
Reports on the Tables of both Houses of Parliament. Out of 185 Reports, only one Report is yet
to be presented to Parliament.
9.2 Department of Legal Affairs forwards Law Commission Reports for examination/
implementation to the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments. Final decision on a law
Commission Report is taken by the concerned Ministries/Departments and not by the Department
of Legal Affairs. Out of 185 Reports, 45 Reports were pending for implementation/consideration
with different concerned Ministries/Departments as on 28 February, 2003. As per the
recommendation of this Committee in its 56th Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000) and 61st
Report on the Demands for Grants (2000-01) of this Ministry, the Department has submitted in
written reply that the concerned Ministries/Departments must be pursued and periodical meetings
with them be called once in a month to look into the progress in regard to the implementation of
the pending Reports, they were pursued through correspondence as well as 49 meetings were held
on various dates in this Department and as a result, the process of consideration/implementation
of the pending Reports has been accelerated. Consultations with State Governments/Union Territory
Administration with a view to implement reports on subjects falling under List-III of Seventh
Schedule to the Constitution are carried on by the concerned administrative Ministries/Departments.

9
9.3 The Committee recommends that the concerned Ministries/Departments may be
prescribed a time bound action plan for implementation of recommendation contained in the
Law Commission Reports pending with them.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
10.0 Legislative Department is one of the oldest Departments, which was set up in the
pre-independence period in 1883 and at one time it was part of the Department of Home. The main
task of the Legislative Department is to draft Bills for enactment of new laws or amendment of
the existing laws and to advise and assist the Administrative Ministries and Departments on
legislative matters at all stages and also to process the Bills at all stages till President’s assent is
received and the Act is published in the Official Gazette.
10.1 Apart from preparing the Bills in the light of the legislative proposals, the Department also
finalises the Statements of Objects and Reasons, Financial Memoranda and the Notes on Clauses,
in connection with introduction of Bills. It also prepares the Memorandum regarding Delegated
Legislation, where required.
10.2 The Department mainly performs the following functions:
(i) It handles the legislative business of the Government of India;
(ii) Administratively handles election laws;
(iii) Administers more than seventy Acts relating to subjects in Concurrent List such as
the Registration Act, the Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, marriage and
divorce, civil procedure, arbitrations, etc.;
(iv) It translates into Hindi, all Central Bills, Acts and translates Constitution of India and
all Central laws into other official languages contained in the VIII Schedule to the
Constitution; and
(v) It bring out reports in Hindi of decisions of the Supreme Court of India and various
High Courts. It also awards prizes for various books in law brought out in Hindi.

Electors Photo Identity Cards
12. The Department has informed the Committee that the targeted campaign period for
achieving 85% target for issue of Electors’ Photo Identity Cards (EPIC), in the 20 States and Union
territories where the electoral rolls have been revised after special revision of intensive nature, was
originally fixed as 31.12.2002, but due to various factors such as flood, famine, administrative and
technical infrastructure and local constraints, the final publication of the electoral rolls in these 20
States was done on different dates between 31.01.2002 to 03.12.2002. As such, a number of States
could not reach the target of 85% by 31.12.2002 and now the Election Commission has asked
them to issue the Electors’ Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) to all the electors not only in respect of
2002 rolls but also in respect of 2003 rolls to be completed by 30.9.2003. It may be mentioned
here that in those States (except Gujarat and Maharashtra), the rolls have been summarily revised
with respect to 01-01-2003. A statement showing the date of final publication of rolls, the total
number of electors, total number of electors issued with EPICs and the percentage thereof is given
at Annexure–II .
12.1 The Election Commission has issued direction for adoption of the following mechanism to
ensure the fulfillment of the above target in these 20 States by 30.09.2003 as under:—
(i) The States, who have not reached the target of 85% by 31.12.2002,  have been asked
to go in for a ‘Campaign Mode’, meaning thereby that wide publicity shall be given
through electronic and print media and also by local methods in the rural areas. The
Chief Electoral Officers of these States have been asked to make in concerted effort
through the district and sub-divisional machinery to reach to the nearest point of the
electors either through on-line method or off-line method. In the on-line method, the
Designated Photographic Location (DPL) Centres are equipped with photographic and
computer infrastructure and the cards are made and provided to the electors on the
same day within 15-25 minutes, while in the off-line method, the cameras are sent
to the nearest point of the electors, to cover as much as possible and bring back
the photographs for processing and making out the cards at processing centers and
thereafter the cards are distributed to the respective electors.
(ii) Those of the States, which have attained the target of  85%, will go in the
‘Maintenance Mode’, whereby the Designated Photographic Location (DPL) Centres
will be provided at the district/sub-divisional headquarters. The electors who will add
to the list later on, will be required to go to these Centres to get their cards
prepared. It is the endeavor of the Commission to achieve the target of issuing the
Electors’ Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) to all the electors by 30.09.2003  in these 20
States through the above mechanism. The Commission is already monitoring the
progress of Electors’ Photo Identity Cards (EPIC) on weekly basis and from time
to time issues directions/clarifications for achieving the target.
12.2 The road map for commencement and completion of the EPIC programme in the 7 States
where special revision of intensive nature has been ordered w.e.f. 01.01.2003 as qualifying date,
is based on the mechanism illustrated above. The dates of final publication of electoral rolls in these

with the Ministry of Home Affairs and Union Home Secretary is ex-officio Secretary, Department
of Justice.
14.1 The principal functions of this Department include appointment of Judges of the Supreme
Court, High Courts and their conditions of service, constitution and organization of the Supreme
Court and establishment of its Benches, review of the strength of Judges, administration of justice
in the Union Territories, monitoring of pendency of cases in Courts including sub ordinate Courts
with a view to expediting their disposal the Department is also responsible for creating Fast Track
Courts, Special Courts, Families Courts, National Judicial Pay Commission (Bangalore) and National
Judicial Academy (Bhopal).
14.2 It is the Nodal Department in so far as the administration of judicial services in States is
concerned, although the actual responsibility of judicial administration below the High Court level
rests with the concerned State Governments and High Courts.

National Judicial Academy (NJA)
17. The National Judicial Academy has been set up for the training for judicial officers of the
States/UTs  and for other related matters. The NJA has been registered under the Societies

15
Registration Act and is an autonomous body. The administration, management and control is vested
in its Governing Council which is chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The building for the
Academy is under construction in Bhopal. It is funded as a central project.
17.1 From 1993-94 to 2001-02, an amount of Rs.79.68 crore was released for the construction
of the Academy building. This includes an amount of Rs.0.53 crore released to the Academy during
1993-94 and 1994-95 for the Secretariat Expenditure of the Academy. The work relating to interior
decoration, design and other remnants is in progress. The Academy has been inaugurated by the
Hon’ble President of India on 5th September, 2002.
17.2 The building has been under construction from 1993-94 to 2001-02 and it is still not fully
functional. Nine years is quite a long period for completion of a building.
17.3 The Committee, therefore, recommends that all requisite steps may be taken by the
concerned authorities so that full fledged functioning of the National Judicial Academy in
the newly constructed building may commence without further delay.
Fast Track Courts
18. The Eleventh Finance Commission, recommended a Scheme for creation of 1734 additional
courts in the country for disposal of long pending sessions and other cases. The Ministry of
Finance sanctioned an amount of Rs.502.90 crore as a special package and upgradation grant for
Judicial Administration. This amount is to be spent over a period of five years, i.e. 2000-05. An
amount of Rs.328.26 crore has been released to various States so far by the Ministry of Finance
for proper implementation of the Scheme. The overall functioning of the Fast Track Courts is the
primary responsibility of the respective State Governments and the concerned High Court. The
cases are transferred to Fast Track Courts under the directions of the respective High Courts.
18.1 Fast Track Courts are taking up sessions cases pending for two years or more and the
cases of under-trials in jails on priority. At present there are about two lakh under-trials in jails on
whose maintenance State Governments are spending about Rs.400 crore per annum at the rate of
Rs.55 per day per person in jail. About 18 per cent of the under-trials are in jail for more than
one year. Such cases are likely to be disposed of by the Fast Track Courts soon. The Scheme
will effect substantial saving in expenditure on jails besides addressing a serious human rights
problem. It will also expedite the disposal of sessions and other cases pending for a long time,
which will have a salutary effect on law and order and crime control. As on 21st February, 2003,
1308 courts have been established out of which 991 courts have already been functioning and they
had disposed of 77,891 cases out of 1,84,207 cases transferred to them.
18.2 The Committee recommends that all out efforts should be made to make all the Fast
Track Courts already notified, functional at the earliest. The Committee is of the view that
the Department of Justice, concerned State Governments and High Courts should evolve an
effective monitoring mechanism to rationalise the pace of disposal of cases by those courts
so that the purpose for which they were created is fulfilled.
Family Courts
19.0 The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a view to providing for the establishment
of Family Courts to promote conciliation in and secure speedy settlement of disputes relating to
marriage, family affairs and related matter.
19.1 Family Cou rts are civil in nature and establishment of which have direct bearing on the
reduction of pendency of civil suits in various High Courts.

16
19.2 In accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, the State/UT Government can
establish Family Courts in the areas comprising district, town, city in the State having population
of ten lakhs. Even States/UTs are competent to establish such Court in those areas with the State/
UT having a population less than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.
19.3 The Department of Justice is the nodal Department mainly responsible for administration of
the said Act.
19.4 Since the enactment of the act i.e. September, 1984 till August, 2001, 84 Family Courts
were established in eighteen States/UT (17 States + 1 UT). Some of the North-Eastern States
(Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Mizoram) do not feel the need for establishment of
such courts as they have lesser number of litigations in relation to family related cases. Moreover,
customary courts are in existence therein to settle those cases. Further there are some UTs
(Laskhadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, Daman and Diu) which have population of less than
10 lakhs also do not have such Courts.
19.5 Further some States viz. Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh have Matrimonial Courts which
decide family related cases exclusively.
19.6 The Central Government started providing financial assistance for construction and running
of Family Courts from the financial year 2002-03 under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme.
19.7 The Department is persuading each State to establish family court in each District. In the
financial year (2002-03) twenty more Family Courts have been set-up, whose details have been

Vacancies of Judges
20. Regarding vacancies of Judges, the Committee in its 86th Report on Demands for Grants
(2002-03) had expressed its serious concern. The Department has informed the Committee that
during the period March 1, 2002 — March 24, 2003, 57 vacancies arose in the High Courts due
to superannuation, death and elevation of High Court judges to Supreme Court. Thus against a total
of 57 vacancies which arose during March 1, 2002 — March 24, 2003, 69 vacancies were filled.
Recommendations for 48 names are under process. During the last three years ( i.e. 2000-01,
2001-02 and 2002-03) the number of vacancies in the High Courts and the appointments made in
the High Courts were as below:
No. of vacancies No. of appointments
2000-01 47 55

(Upto 24 March, 2003)
20.1 The Department has also stated that the number of appointments has been higher than the
number of retirements. Thus significant improvement has been made towards filling up vacancies
of Judges in the High Courts.
20.2 The Department has further stated that the Chief Justices of the High Courts are being
requested from time to time to send their recommendations to fill up the vacancies in their High
Courts. A statement showing the vacancy positive (High Court wise) as on 28.2.03 is placed at
Annexure IV .
20.3 Inspite of best efforts by the Department, it may be highlighted that still there are about
136 vacancies out of total approved strength i.e. 547 in various High Courts.
20.4 The Judges of the High Courts were appointed by the President after consultation with the
Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and in the case of appointment of a Judge other
than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of the High Court vide article 217 (1) of the Constitution.
Before 1993, the process of appointment of Judges of High Courts and Supreme Court was
required to be initiated by the Executive i.e. Department of Justice, as far as possible 6 months
prior to the date of vacancy. There were delays in filling the vacancies during that period also
but the Government was answerable and accountable to Parliament. After the Judgement of
the Supreme Court in Advocates-on-Record Association vs. Union of India and others on
October 6,  1993, a proposal for appointment of a  Judge cannot be initiated by the  Government.
According to the Judgement of October 6, 1993, read with the Advisory Opinion of
October 28, 1998, of the Supreme Court of India, the initiation of the proposal for appointment
of a Judge of the Supreme Court must be by the Chief Justice of India and in the case of a Judge
of the High  Court by the Chief Justice of that High Court. For transfer of a Judge/Chief Justice
of a High Court to another High Court, the proposal has to be initiated by the Chief Justice of
India.
20.5 The Government is now committed to setting up of a National Judicial Commission, which
would make recommendations for appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and the High
Courts, as also draw up a Code of Ethics for Judges. The National Commission to Review the
Working of the Constitution has recommended (Para 7.3.7) for setting up the National Judicial
Commission for the Supreme Court only.

18
20.6 The Committee had recommended in its 86th Report to take steps to restore the pre-1993
position of appointment of judges of Supreme Court and High Courts be introduced The
Government feels that the conflicting opinions on the merit of the 1993 judgement would get
resolved by the establishment of the proposed National Judicial Commission through an amendment
to the relevant articles of the Constitution of India.
20.7 The Government has taken steps to build up a consensus on the proposed establishment of
the National Judicial Commission. Political parties have been requested to communicate their views
on various aspects of the proposed National Judicial Commission.
20.8 The Committee would like to impress upon the Government to take suitable action
at the earliest to restore the pre-1993 position in the matter of appointment of Judges in
Supreme Court and High Courts, by bringing in, if necessary a suitable legislation.
Benches of Supreme Court
21. The Committee in its meeting held on 21st March, 2003 was of the view that the reply of
the Supreme Court regarding setting up of Benches of Supreme Court in far-flung areas with a
view to provide justice to poor people for whom it is impossible to go to the National Capital, was
not convincing and felt that setting up of Benches outside Delhi would neither impair the unity and
integrity nor undermine the importance of the Supreme Court. Rather on the other hand, it would
send a message of integration and a sense of belonging in the country.
The Department in its written reply, has informed the Committee as under:
“Representations have been received from time to time from various Bar Associations etc.
for establishment of Benches of Supreme Court in various parts of the country. Suggestions
have also been made by the Governments of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka,
Tripura and West Bengal for establishment of Benches of the Supreme Court for Southern/
Eastern and North-Eastern parts of the country. The Law Ministers of Eastern and North-
Eastern States adopted a resolution unanimously in their meeting held on October 4, 1996
in Calcutta that it is essential for the Supreme Court to sit at a suitable place in their region.
The matter has been referred to the Chief Justice of India from time to time. The Supreme
Court has been opposed to setting up of a Bench of the Supreme Court at any place outside
Delhi. In its communication dated April 26, 1997 received from the Registry of the Supreme
Court, it was stated that the suggestions for establishment of Benches of the Supreme Court
outside Delhi had been considered and disapproved by the Full Court in a meeting presided
over by the Chief Justice of India.
The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, while discussing the Demands for
Grants of the Ministry of Law and Justice for 1999-2000 in its 56th Report recommended
that Government should think of setting up Benches of Supreme Court in Southern, Western
and North-Eastern parts of the country.
The recommendation was conveyed to the Chief Justice of India for his views in terms of
article 130 of the Constitution of India. The Chief Justice of India intimated vide his letter
dated 3rd February, 2000 that having regard to the importance of the matter the subject was
discussed in a Full Court meeting of the Hon’ble Judges of Supreme Court held on
15th December, 1999. The Full Court after due deliberations, unanimously reiterated its
stand already taken on the subject in its Resolutions dated 18th August, 1984, 11th May, 1994
and 18th March, 1997 opposing the setting up of the Benches and Filing Section of the
Supreme Court outside Delhi.

19
The views of the Full Court opposing the setting up of the Benches of the Supreme Court
outside Delhi were brought to the notice of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee. The Committee in its 61st and 72nd report reiterated its recommendations made
in its 56th Report for setting up of Benches in the Southern, Western and North-Eastern
parts of the country so that the people of far-flung areas get easy access to the Apex
Court. The Committee also urged upon the Government to again take up the matter with
the Chief Justice of India.
The above recommendation of the Parliamentary Committee was communicated to the Chief
Justice of India on 29th June, 2000.
The Chief Justice of India has conveyed vide his letter dated 2nd May, 2001 that the matter
was discussed in a Full Court meeting of Hon’ble Judges on 30th April, 2001 which after
thorough reconsideration of the issue unanimously found no justification in deviating from
their earlier resolutions on the subject. Accordingly, the Full Court did not accept the
demand of the Department related Parliamentary Committee regarding setting up of Benches
of the Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-Eastern parts of the country”.
22. The Committee having noted the written replies of the Department of Justice once
again reiterates its recommendation for setting up of Benches of Supreme Court outside
Delhi and request the Government to approach the Chief Justice of India for
reconsideration by the Supreme Court of its earlier decision in the matter, as the
Committee strongly feels that establishment of Benches of Supreme Court in Southern,
Western and North-Eastern parts of the country would facilitate the litigants to avail justice
from the apex court without travelling to Delhi from far away places.
Pendency of Cases
23. The High Court of Allahabad has the highest pendency i.e. 909641 as on 31.3.2002. The
Department of Justice has stated that the pendency of cases in courts is, inter-alia, due to various
factors including shortage of judges, increased institution of cases on account of increased
awareness of rights on the part of citizens, rise in population, new laws, granting of adjournments,
industrial development of the country, increase in trade and commerce and socio-economic matters,
legislative and administrative aspects touching on the life of the citizens at all levels, tendency of
litigants, lawyers’ strike etc. Statements indicating the pendency in High Courts and sub-ordinate
Courts are enclosed at Annexures IV and V .
23.1 The Government has further stated that various measures have been adopted by the High
Courts for expeditious disposal of cases including classification and grouping of cases,
computerization of records in High Courts, identification and listing of cases covered by the
decisions finally made by the Supreme Court and High Court on the same point.
23.2 The Minister of Law and Justice has been requesting Chief Justices of High Courts from
time to time, to initiate proposals for filling up vacancies of Judges in the High Courts.
23.3 Government has been compiling analysis reports on pendency of cases both criminal and
civil in High Courts and District Courts and forwarding them to the High Courts for their
information and necessary action. High Courts have been requested to implement the
recommendations of the Malimath Committee to streamline procedures which will, inter-alia,
expedite disposal of pending cases. Government have also been constantly reviewing the
accumulation of arrears in courts. Besides reviewing and increasing judges’ strength of High Courts
every three years, Government have set up/encouraged alternative modes of dispute resolution
including conciliation, mediation and arbitration. Special tribunals like Central Administrative
Tribunal, State Administrative Tribunals, Income Tax, Appellate Tribunal, Labour Courts, Consumer

20
Courts, Family Courts, etc., have been set up to expedite the disposal of cases. Information
Technology is being used in generation of causelists, providing information to the litigants/advocates
etc., for speedy disposal of cases. A Pilot project has been started for Networking and
Computerisation of City Courts in the four major metro cities of Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata and
Mumbai to serve as a model. The purpose of this project is to augment the capacities of courts
and speed up adjudication through better court management with the use of information technology.
23.4 This year the Department of Justice is initiating a pilot project of upgrading the computer
network of the four metropolitan High Courts of Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras to the level
of the Supreme Court so as to bring about the same speed and efficiency in disposal of cases in
these High Courts as exists in the Supreme Court.
23.5 Civil Procedure Code has been amended and the amendments have been brought into force
with effect from 1.07.2002 which, inter-alia , limit the number of adjournments which can be
granted to a party to three, provide for speedy process service by speed post, courier services,
fax or e-mail, authorise the court to fix time limit for oral arguments and provide for a number
of other measures aimed at ensuring expeditious disposal of cases. Permanent Lok Adalats are being
set up for expeditious resolution of disputes relating to public utilities.
23.6 Huge arrears of cases in the High Court and Sub-ordinate courts is a matter of
serious concern. The Committee having noted the various steps taken to reduce the arrears
in courts, urges upon the Government to consider initiating other new measures to arrest
pendency of cases.

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this Hundred-second Report of the Committee on the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution
(Amendment) Bill, 2003 and the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Bill, 2003.*
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha referred** the
two Bills, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 9 May, 2003 and pending therein, to the Committee
for examination and report.
3. The Committee considered both the Bills in its sitting held on 26 June and 14 July, 2003.
3.1 The Committee took oral evidence of representatives of Ministry of Home Affairs in its
sitting held on 26 June, 2003. In the same sitting, the Committee discussed the general principles
of the Bills and also took up clause-by-clause consideration thereof.
3.2 The Committee considered the draft Report on the Bills and adopted the same in its meeting
held on 14 July, 2003
4. In the course of its deliberations, the Committee has made use of the background notes on
the Bills and other relevant documents received from the Ministry of Home Affairs and replies of
the Ministry to the queries raised by the Members in its sitting.
5. For facility of reference and convenience, observations and recommendations of the
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.
