CHAPTER-I
The Sixth Schedule to the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, 2003
The Bill seeks to create an autonomous self-governing body to be known as the Bodoland
Territorial Council (BTC) within the State of Assam under Schedule VI of the Constitution of India
which shall have legislative, administrative and financial powers in respect of specified subjects.
The Bill further seeks to provide for adequate safeguards for the non-tribals in the BTC areas in
regard to rights and privileges including land rights presently enjoyed by them at the
commencement of BTC.
2. During his deposition before the Committee on 26 June, 2003, the Joint Secretary (NE),
Ministry of Home Affairs traced the genesis of the Bill and informed the Committee that the Bodos
were the largest recognized plain tribe in Assam comprising 1.2 million people or 5.3 % of the total
population of Assam of 22.4 million as per 1991 census. They were chiefly inhabitants of Dhubri,
Kokrajhar, Bongaigaon, Barpeta, Nalbari, Kamrup and Darrang Districts of Assam.
2.1 He also apprised the Committee that the Bodo problem primarily arose due to perception of
negligence of the Bodo areas by successive Governments in Assam since independence, influx of
migrants from other parts of Assam, West Bengal, Bihar and Bangladesh, which led to alienation
of tribal land, though prohibited by the Assam Land Revenue (Rules and Regulations) 1886 and
search for separate Bodo identity. The proposed BTC areas would also include other tribes living
in Deori, Hojai, Kachari including Sonowal, Lalung, Mech, Miri and Rabha.
3. He further stated that in order to address and solve the Bodo problem, the Government of
India signed the Bodo Accord on February 20, 1993 with All Bodo Students Union and Bodo
People’s Action Committee with the following salient features:
(i) a Bodoland Autonomous Council (BAC) to be formed by an Act of Assam Legislative
Assembly;
(ii) the Council to have powers to make bylaws, rules and orders for application within
the BAC areas on the specified subjects;
(iii) the geographical area of the BAC as agreed upon can be changed with the mutual
consent of the BAC and the Government of Assam;
(iv) the BAC will have power to regulate trade and commerce within its jurisdiction, in
accordance with the existing laws;
(v) the Government of Assam will deposit in the BAC fund, revenue collected from the
tea gardens falling within the BAC area;
(vi) the BAC would also receive grant-in-aid from time to time within the principles and
policies enunciated by the Government of India; and
(vii) the Government of Assam and the BAC will jointly ensure that all rights and interests
of the non-tribals as on date living in the BAC area in matters pertaining to land as
well as their language are protected.
3.1 In pursuance of the Bodo Accord, the BAC Act was passed by the Legislative Assembly of
Assam which came into force on 13 May, 1993. The Act provided for the establishment of an

2
administrative authority known as Bodoland Autonomous Council (BAC) and for certain matters
incidental and connected thereto.
3.2 The Joint Secretary further stated that the BAC had, however, failed to achieve the
objectives for which it was set up and the Bodo groups were of the view that Bodo Accord had
become unworkable due to non-implementation of the Accord in letter and spirit and were making
renewed demands for separate State of Bodoland for the following reasons.
(i) No elections could be held to the General Council of BAC so far;
(ii) There was also dispute over the areas to be included in the BAC;
(iii) BAC had no legislative powers; and
(iv) Allocation and transfer of adequate funds for development works to BAC was not
assured.
3.3 Thus, the BAC had failed to achieve the objectives for which it was set up leading to
renewed demand for separate State of Bodoland.
4. It was against this backdrop that the Government of India initiated a fresh process of
dialogue with the Bodos in September, 1997. In  response to the initiative of the Central
Government, the Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) unilaterally suspended its operations with effect
from 14 July, 1999. This was followed by a series of tripartite talks between Government of India,
Government of Assam and BLT. After twenty one rounds of tripartite talks, a Memorandum of
Settlement (MoS) was signed on 10 February, 2003. The main terms of agreement inter alia
include:
(i) Creation of an Autonomous District to be known as Bodoland Territorial Council
(BTC) Areas D istrict within the State of Assam and provision of Constitutional
protection under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India;
(ii) The Government of Assam to repeal the BAC Act, 1993 and dissolve the existing
Bodoland Autonomous Council (BAC);
(iii) Adequate safeguards to ensure that the non-tribals in the BTC area are not
disadvantaged in relation to any rights and privileges including land rights presently
enjoyed by them at the commencement of BTC;
(iv) Increasing the number of members for BTC upto 46 out of which 30 will be
reserved for Scheduled Tribes, 5 for non-tribal communities, 5 open for all
communities and 6 to be nominated by Governor of Assam from the unrepresented
communities from BTC area of which at least 2 should be women. Nominated
members will have the same rights and privileges as other members, including voting
rights. Election for 40 constituencies of the BTC shall be on the basis of adult
franchise. The term of the elected members of the BTC shall be for 5 years;
(v) The Council shall have legislative, executive, administrative and financial powers in
respect of 40 subjects to be entrusted to it;
(vi) Additional financial assistance of Rs. 100 crore per annum (over and above normal
plan assistance to the State of Assam) for next five years for projects to develop the
socio-economic infrastructure in BTC areas;
(vii) The Government of India has also agreed to consider favourably the inclusion of
Bodo language in Devnagri script in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution;

3
(viii) A C entrally funded Central Institute of Technology (CIT) to be set up to impart
education in various technologies and vocational disciplines such as information
technology, bio-technology, food processing, rural industries, business management,
etc. The CIT to be subsequently upgraded to a centrally-funded State University with
technical and non-technical disciplines to be run by the BTC; and
(ix) The Government of India to consider sympathetically the inclusion of Boro Kacharis
living in Karbi Anglong and North Cachar Hills Autonomous Councils area in the
Scheduled Tribes (Hill) List of State of Assam.
5. Here, it may be pertinent to compare the distinct features of the proposed BTC under the
Sixth Schedule to the Constitution and the BAC under the State Act;
(i) The BTC will be created under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India
whereas the BAC was created under the State Legislation;
(ii) The number of members for the BTC will be 46, out of which 30 will be reserved
for Scheduled Tribes, 5 for non-tribal communities, 5 open for all communities from
BTC areas of which at least 2 will be women. On the other hand, the number of
members of BAC was 40, of which, 30 seats were reserved for Scheduled Tribes
and 10 seats were open seats;
(iii) BTC will have a defined territory whereas BAC territory was not defined:
(iv) Elections will be ensured in BTC after every five years, while no elections could
take place in BAC in the last ten years;
(v) BTC will have legislative powers over specified subjects which was not so with
BAC;
(vi) Adequate safeguards for the non-tribals in regard to rights enjoyed by them including
land rights have been provided in the BTC and the existing representation of
Scheduled Tribes and non-scheduled tribes from BTC area in the State Assembly is
to be kept intact.
6. Further, while touching upon the earmarked area and population of the proposed BTC, the
Joint Secretary stated that 3082 villages were to be included in the BTC area. Besides, a decision
was to be taken to add 95 more villages in it. He informed that the total area of BAC as against
proposed BTC included 2941 villages and approximately 8300 sq. kms. of land with a population
of around 25 lakhs. Out of which total Bodo population was 9.84 lakhs. However, the area as well
as population of the proposed BTC may undergo slight change with the increase in number of
villages.
7. The Joint Secretary also apprised the Committee of the steps already taken by the
Government to implement the Memorandum of Settlement such as repeal of BAC Act, 1993 and
dissolution of BAC by the State Government, agreement on 3082 villages to be included in BTC,
consideration of proposal for grant of Scheduled Tribe (Hill) status to Boro Kacharis living in North
Cachar Hill and Karbi Anglong districts as also the proposal for inclusion of Bodo language in the
Eighth Schedule to the Constitution. The allocation of Rs.100 crore per annum to BTC and
establishment of centrally funded Central Institute of Technology was also under consideration of
the Government.
7.1 While justifying further the inclusion of proposed BTC in the Sixth Schedule to the
Constitution, he drew the attention of the Committee to the recommendation of the National
Commission to review the working of the Constitution that the Sixth Schedule should be extended
to the BAC with protection for non-tribal and non-Bodo groups.

4
8. Before winding up the presentation, the Home Secretary proposed further additions/
amendments in the Bill which was under consideration of the Committee Explaining the need for
additions/amendments in the Bill, the Joint Secretary stated that in the State of Assam, Scheduled
Tribes were divided into two categories viz. Scheduled Tribes of Autonomous Districts and
Scheduled Tribes of areas other than Autonomous Districts. Bodo Kacharis were at present
included in the list of Scheduled Tribes of areas other than Autonomous Districts and were
popularly known as Scheduled Tribes (Plains). Consequent upon the formation of BTC Area District
and its inclusion in the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution of India, the Bodo Kacharis residing in
the plain districts of Assam would stand disqualified from the Scheduled Tribes (Plains) status. In
order that Bodo Kacharis continue to enjoy the Scheduled Tribes status, amendments were
proposed to be carried out in the Schedule to the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes Order, 1950) in
Part-II Assam as under:
(a) In item No.I “in the Autonomous Districts” be substituted by “in the Autonomous
Districts of Karbi Anglong and North Cachar Hills”.
(b) In item No.II for “in the State of Assam excluding the Autonomous Districts” be
substituted by “in the State of Assam including the Bodoland Territorial Council Areas
District and excluding the Autonomous Districts of Karbi Anglong and North Cachar
Hills”.
8.1 He informed the Committee that the proposed additions/amendments would be included in
the Bill as “Miscellaneous Provisions”.
9. After due deliberations, the Committee expressed its whole hearted support to give
a fair trial to the tripartite agreement signed by the Government of India, Government of
Assam and the Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) on 10 February, 2003 by way of the proposed
legislation.
10. The Committee then took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.
11. The Committee having adopted the clauses of the Bill without any amendments and
having approved the Government amendments to be included as ‘Miscellaneous Provisions’
in the Bill, recommends that it may be passed.

CHAPTER-II
The Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Bill, 2003
This Bill is a natural corollary to the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution (Amendment)
Bill, 2003 which has been dealt with in Chapter-I of this Report. Accordingly, this Chapter is
devoted to the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Bill, 2003. This Bill has also emanated from
the Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) signed between the Government of India, Government of
Assam and Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) on 10 February, 2003. It fulfills one of the terms of the
agreement which reads as under:
“Provisions of Article 332(6) of the Constitution will be so modified that the existing status
of representation of BTC area in the State Assembly is kept intact. After the creation of
BTC, the Parliamentary and  Assembly Constituencies shall be delimited by the Delimitation
Commission in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.”
1.1 Thus, this term of the MoS seeks to protect the existing status of representation of
proposed BTC area in the State Assembly by way of amending Article 332(6) of the Constitution.
2. Before having a look at the provisions of the proposed Bill, it may be pertinent to delve into
Article 332(6) of the Constitution. It stipulates that no person who is not a member of a Scheduled
Tribe of any autonomous district of the State of Assam shall be eligible for election to the
Legislative Assembly of the State from any constituency of that district.
2.1 Thus, Article 332(6) prohibits election of non-tribals to the State Legislative Assembly from
the constituencies which fall within an autonomous district. Now with the creation of one more
autonomous district in the State of Assam, namely, Bodoland Territorial Council Area District, the
provision under Article 332(6) will also apply mutatis mutandis  to it unless it is amended or
modified otherwise. In other words, if the provision under Article 332 (6) is not amended, it will
deprive the non-tribals living in BTC area of their representation in the State Assembly. Hence, the
need for amendment.
3. Against this backdrop, this Bill seeks to insert a proviso in clause 6 of Article 332 of the
Constitution which aims at protecting the political rights of the non-tribals by ensuring that the
existing representation of scheduled tribes and non-scheduled tribes from the proposed BTC areas
in the State Assembly remains intact.
4. The Home Secretary along with other officials made a brief power point presentation on the
Bill before the Committee in its meeting held on 26 June, 2003.
5. The Committee also took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill in the same meeting.
6. The Committee, having adopted the Bill without any amendments, recommends that
it may be passed.

and the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Bill, 2003. The Committee, then, took up for
consideration the draft Hundred and Second Report on the Bills. The Chairman also invited
suggestions and comments the Members present on the draft Report.
2.1 A Member raised a query with regard to giving Bodos living in North Cachar districts the
Scheduled Tribe (Plain) status as well as the Scheduled Tribe (Hill) status. The Chairman informed
that the matter had already been clarified by the Home Secretary that it was separately under
consideration and no decision on it had been taken so far.
2.2 After some discussion, the Committee adopted the draft Report without any change.
3. The Committee then took up discussion on the constitution ninety-seventh (Amendment)
Bill, 2003. The Chairman welcomed Joint Secretary (Legislative Department) to the meeting and
made general observations on the subject matter of the Bill, and thereafter, left the floor to other
Members to express their views on the Bill.
3.1 Majority of the Members present, participated in the debate on the Bill. All of them
supported the Bill and some of them even went to the extent of suggesting amendments to make
the law more stringent.
3.2 The Chairman and some other Members opined that the decision of the Presiding Officer
in regard to disqualification of Members cannot be challenged in any Court as enumerated in para
7 of Tenth Schedule to the Constitution. Some Members opined that adjudication of issues within
the House could not be entrusted to an outside authority and appeal against the decision of the
Speaker/Chairman could be made to the President and not to the judiciary.
3.3 A Member was of the view that political parties, with reference to split, should mean both
the political wing as well as the legislative wing of the party. He was of the view that in order
to make the anti-defection law effective, it was imperative to cure the malady. He was of the view
that the political system may be strengthened by having inner party democracy and by maintaining
judicious balance between individual conscience of the legislator and party discipline. The Member
further stated that whip should be issued only on matters of great importance such as — when
there was no-confidence motion, financial business, etc.
3.4 Some Members opined that if the vote of an MP/MLA was against party manifesto and
caused fall of the Government, then he/she should be disqualified and also that the ratio for Upper
House and Lower House for Ministership should be fixed within the 10% limit prescribed in the
proposed legislation. Freedom of action of any Member may be confined to the areas which do
not violate party’s ideology/manifesto/activity/symbol.
3.5 Other Members who felt that the size of the Council of Ministers should be 5-7% and not
10% of the total strength of the Legislature. Also that the Constitution should be amended to
provide that the Member who defects and joins another party, should stand automatically
disqualified from the membership of the House and debarred from holding any post. An
apprehension was also expressed with regard to the provision of the Bill relating to limiting the size

15
of the Council of Ministers to 10% of the membership of the two Houses of the Parliament/
Legislative Assembly, such as a provision was likely to put the unicameral States at disadvantage.
Such States with unicameral legislature may demand for the Upper House—the Legislative Council,
to be at par with the bicameral States w.r.t. the size of the Council of Ministers. On the other hand,
a Member expressed the view, that considering many new subjects and areas of activities which
come up like WTO, etc. limit of 10% should not be fixed for the size of the Council of Ministers.
3.6 Another Member added that Presiding Officers sometimes take long time to arrive at a
decision regarding disqualification of a member and at times take such decisions very expeditiously.
Therefore, the decision of Presiding Officer relating to disqualification should be time-bound.
3.7 One Member, while expressing concern, that of late, defection was causing instability in
bigger States like U.P. and Bihar which was earlier confined to smaller States and the possibility
for defection even after this amendment, as the defectors could be accommodated in the Council
of Ministers through the other route i.e., by offering a seat in Rajya Sabha/Upper House in the
States and suggested that stringent law was which debarred requested defectors who later become
Members of the Rajya Sabha, to get the post of Ministership.
4. The chairman, then thanked Members for the animated discussion. He suggested that
another round of discussion may be held to enable those Members who were not present, to
participate in the discussion.
5. A verbatim record of the proceeding was kept.
6. The meeting then adjourned at 5.44

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The provisions of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution have evolved a
separate scheme for the governance of the tribal areas in the S tates of Assam,
Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura through the District Councils or Regional
Councils. There are three parts in the Table appended to the Schedule. They are
so divided in order to distinguish the Areas. The Areas in Part I represent the
Tribal Areas of Assam. Each of these Areas constitutes an “autonomous district”.
The provisions in paragraphs 1 to 17 of the Sixth Schedule relate to the
Administration of these autonomous districts. The Councils are vested with
legislative powers on specified subjects and are allotted sources of taxation.
They have also been given powers to set up and administer their system of
justice and maintain administrative and welfare services in respect of land,
revenue, forests, education, public health, etc.
2. The Bodo Accord was signed on February 20, 1993 with All Bodo
Students Union and Bodo People’s Action Committee, with the objective to
provide maximum autonomy to the Bodos within the framework of the
Constitution for their social, economic, educational and cultural advancement. In
pursuance to the Bodo Accord, an Interim Bodoland Autonomous Council (BAC)
was constituted by the Government of Assam by enacting State Legislation.
Bodo groups were of the view that Bodo Accord had become unworkable due
to non-implementation of the Accord in letter and spirit. Based on the tripartite
talks, a Memorandum of Settlement (MoS) has been signed between the Central
Government, the Government of Assam and Bodo Liberation Tigers (BLT) on
10.2.2003 for a durable solution to the Bodo issues.
3. To meet the aspirations of the Bodos in Assam and in pursuance of the
MoS, it is proposed to—
(i) create an autonomous self-governing body to be known as the
Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) within the State of Assam, which shall
have legislative, administrative and financial powers in respect of specified
subjects;
(ii) provide for adequate safeguards for the non-tribals in the BTC
area to ensure that they are not put to any disadvantage in relation to any
rights and privileges including land rights presently enjoyed by them at the
commencement of BTC.
4. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
Article 332 of the Constitution of India provides for reservation of seats for
the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in the Legislative Assemblies of
the States. Clause (6) of article 332 stipulates that no person who is not a
member of a Scheduled Tribe of any autonomous district of the State of Assam
shall be eligible for election to the Legislative Assembly of the State from any
constituency of that district.
2. In pursuance of the Memorandum of Settlement signed on the 10th day
of February, 2003 between the Government of India, Government of Assam and
Bodo Liberation Tigers, and to protect the rights of the non-tribals, the existing
representation of the Scheduled Tribes and non-Scheduled Tribes in the
Legislative Assembly of the State of Assam from the Bodoland Territorial Council
Areas District is proposed to be kept intact. It is, therefore, proposed to insert
a proviso in clause (6) of article 332 of the Constitution.
3. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

1
REPORT
The Salaries and Allowances of the Judicial Officers of the Union Territories Bill, 2003
(Annexure-I) intends to prescribe scales of pay for the Judicial Officers in the Union Territories
and also to introduce a Special Judicial Allowance (SJA) @ 10 per cent of the Basic Pay as
compensation for their duties which involve essential work such as reading, referencing, dictating
judgements and preparing for cases, etc. beyond normal working hours of Courts.
2.0 In the backdrop of the proposed legislation, there lie circumstances, which led to several
attempts by the Union Government to regulate service conditions of Judicial Officers of UTs.
2.1 It goes back to the Writ Petition (Civil) No.1022 of 1989 filed by the All India Judges’
Association before the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking reliefs
so as to improve the conditions of service of Subordinate Judicial Officers all over the country.
2.2 In the case of All India Judges Association versus Union of India and others (AIR 1992 SC
165) the Supreme Court on 13 November, 1991 d irected the Union Government to evolve an
appropriate National Policy in regard to the service conditions of the Judicial Officers. In pursuance
of the directions of the Supreme Court, while disposing Review Petition filed by the Union
Government, on 24 August, 1993 (AIR 1993 SC 2493), the Union Government by Resolution dated
21 March, 1996 constituted the First National Judicial Pay Commission (FNJPC) under the
Chairmanship of Justice K. Jagannath Shetty for the Sub- ordinate Judiciary all over the country
with the following terms of reference:—
(a) To evolve the principles which should govern the structure of pay and other
emoluments of Judicial Officers belonging to the Subordinate Judiciary all over the
country;
(b) To examine the present structure of emoluments and conditions of service of Judicial
officers in the States and UTs taking into account the total packet of benefits
available to them and make suitable recommendations having regard, among other
relevant factors, to the existing relativities in the pay structure between the officers
belonging to subordinate judicial service vis-a-vis other civil servants.
(c) To examine and recommend in respect of minimum qualifications, age of
recruitment, method of recruitment etc., for Judicial Officers. In this context, the
relevant provisions of the Constitution and direction of the Supreme Court in All
India Judges’ Association Case and in other cases may be kept in view.
(d) To examine the work methods and work environment as also the variety of
allowances and benefits in kind that are available to Judicial Officers in addition to
pay and to suggest rationalisation and simplification thereof with a view to promoting
efficiency in Judicial Administration, optimising the size of the Judiciary etc.
2.3 As the Fifth Central Pay Commission did not consider the issue of revised salary structure
and allowances of subordinate judiciary, the Union Government added a term of reference on
16 December, 1997 to consider pay package and grant interim relief pending recommendations of
the FNJPC, on the condition that the interim relief so recommended was to be adjusted against the
pay package admissible to the judicial officers as contained in the final recommendation of the
FNJPC. The FNJPC through its Interim Report dated 31 January, 1998 granted Interim Relief to
the Judicial Officers of States and Union Territories. The FNJPC submitted its Report (three
volumes) to the Government on 11 November, 1999.

2
3. The FNJPC has made wide-ranging recommendations covering salary structure, emoluments
and other conditions of service of judicial of ficers throughout the country. Those recommendations
were considered and partially implemented by the Union Government on 11 October, 2001 in
respect of judicial officers of Union Territories for which the Union Government is administratively
responsible, by granting pay scales keeping in view traditional relativities and parity between pay
scales of the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) with that of subordinate judiciary
3.1 The Supreme Court in its judgement of 21 March, 2002 in All India Judges Association case
(2002 (4) SCC 247) directed that the pay scales recommended by the First National Judicial Pay
Commission should be accepted in toto . The Court observed that considering the years of service
the judicial officers put in at different stages, the pay scales recommended by the Commission
should be wholly accepted, regardless of the IAS scales. The Court, however, rejected the
recommendation that the Union Government should bear fifty per cent of the expenditure since the
responsibility of the subordinate judiciary, except for that of the Union Territories, was exclusively
with the States. Further, the Supreme Court in its order dated 25 November, 2002 reiterated that
the higher pay scales of the officers of subordinate judiciary must be implemented, on or before
1 April, 2003.
3.2 After considering the judgement of the Supreme Court, the Union Cabinet on 31 March, 2003
decided to bring legislation under Article 309 of the Constitution to regulate the salary and service
conditions of the Judicial Officers in Union Territories. The Cabinet also decided to introduce a
Special Judicial Allowance at the rate of 10 per cent of the basic pay to the judicial officers of
Union Territories as compensation for their duties which involve essential work beyond normal
working hours of Courts, which was communicated to the Supreme Court through an affidavit of
the Department of Justice on 8 May, 2003.
3.3 A comparison amongst pay scales recomended by the FNJPC, pay scales granted by the
Union Government as interim measure and those proposed in the Bill alongwith Special Judicial
Allowance are shown in the Annexure-II.
3.4 In the meanwhile, the High Powered Committee for assessing the fiscal situation of the
States, which met on 9 August, 2002 under the Chairmanship of Union Minister of Finance and
Company Affairs expressed the apprehension that in addition to the direct impact due to revision
of pay scales and sanction of allowances recommended by the FNJPC, there would be considerable
impact on the States’ Finances as existing parities would get disturbed and the employees would
also demand extension of allowances similar to what was provided to the Judicial Offices. The
High Powered Committee pleaded that the Union Government should keep in view the States’
concern while taking a decision on the application of pay scales of Judicial Officers in the Union
Territories. Thereafter, in the meeting convened by the Ministry of Finance on 7 September, 2002,
the State Finance Ministers expressed serious difficulties regarding the constitutional, financial and
administrative issues involved in implementing the Supreme Court’s judgement of 21 March, 2002
in the All India Judges Association case relating to pay scales and other service conditions of the
subordinate judiciary. It was resolved that States will take appropriate action in the State
Legislatures through resolution or any other alternative legislative measure. A meeting of Chief
Ministers of States and the Prime Minister held on 18 October, 2002, also ratified this decision.
3.5. However, many State Governments complied with the directions of the Supreme Court of
21 March, 2002 and orders of 25 November, 2002 and 9 May, 2003 in All India Judges Association
case in respect of pay scales by means of executive orders. The Table showing the list of States,
which have implemented the recommendations of the FNJPC in respect of pay scales of Judicial
Officers, may be seen at Annexure VII.
3.6 The total number of Judicial Officers who would be benefitted by the proposed legislation
are 3437. The detailed breakup of the beneficiaries (UT-wise) is given at Annexure-III.

3
4. The Home Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on 23 June, 2003 had stated
that the proposed Bill, if enacted by the Parliament, would ensure:—
(i) that existing traditional relativities with similar central cadres are not disturbed;
(ii) supremacy of the Parliament/Legislature; and
(iii) will act as a role model for other States to follow the legislation if they so choose.
5.0 The All India Judges Association, Hyderabad had submitted a memorandum dated
11 August, 2003 (Annexure IV) to the Committee on the issues pertaining to the Bill and requested
that Shri Justice C. Sri Ramulu (Retd. Judge, Andhra Pradesh High Court) and Shri C.K.
Chaturvedi (Additional District and Sessions Judge, Delhi), Chairman and Working President of the
Association, respectively, may be provided an opportunity of giving oral evidence before the
Committee on the Bill. The Committee acceded to their request and heard their views on the Bill
in its meeting held on 3 September, 2003. The Association also submitted their written Affidavit
Evidence (Annexures V and VI) to the Committee in the said meeting. During the meeting, the
Committee sought some clarification on the points arising out of their evidence and requested them
to send their written responses. In pursuance of the Committee’s direction, the Association
submitted an additional Memorandum dated 9 September, 2003 (Annexure VII).  The Memoranda
dated 11 August and 9 September, 2003 and Affidavit Evidence dated 3 September, 2003 were
forwarded to the Department of Justice for their comments.
5.1 The Association inter alia raised the following main points:—
(i) The proposed Bill is in gross violation of the Judgements of the Supreme Court. The
Association is of the view that the Union Government has no right to introduce the
Bill to set at naught the legal effect of three judgments of Supreme Court to which
the Union of India is a party. The Government must implement in letter and spirit
the recommendations of the FNJPC and orders of the Supreme Court thereon
recommending pay structure of Subordinate Judiciary on an uniform pattern all over
the country.
(ii) The Government of India cannot itself take the place of expert body and frame its
own pay scales when the terms of reference of the FNJPC was to evolve the
uniform salary structure for the Judicial Officers of the entire country. Since the
proposed pay scales for the Judicial Officers of the Union Territories are contrary
to the pay structure recommended by the FNJPC and accepted by the State
Governments, it would create anomaly thereby causing disparities in the pay scales
of Judicial Officers in the States and Union Territories.
(iii) It was apprehended that the proposed legislation may pave the way for the States
to introduce similar type of legislation which would be against the recommendations
of the FNJPC and the orders of the Supreme Court. As such Himachal Pradesh is
waiting for such an opportunity.
5.2 Replying to the queries posed by the Committee, the All India Judges Association further
submitted the following points:—
(i) Comparison of pay scales should not be between the judiciary and the executive. It
can be better understood keeping in view the identifiable grades and levels of
responsibility and promotional avenues in the judicial service only.
(ii) The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill admitting the onerous nature of
responsibilities assigned to the Judicial Officers, makes an attempt to treat an officer
doing judicial and non-judicial work on equal footing.

4
(iii) There is no enabling provision in the Bill to enable the Government to revise in future
the salaries based on recommendations of FNJPC.
(iv) The Bill has been introduced at a time when the matter is still pending in Supreme
Court in respect of some clarifications on Assured Career Progression Scheme and
other allowances, which are awaited from Union of India.
5.3 The Association, therefore, requested the Committee to consider removing the disparities by
recommending to the Union of India to implement the recommendations of FNJPC in letter and
spirit and uniformly.
5.4 The Department of Justice offered their comments (Annexure VIII) on the points raised
by the All India Judges Association as under:—
(i) The Bill maintains traditional parity and relativities in the pay scales between the
executive and the judiciary. The SJA proposed in the Bill is to compensate the
onerous duties performed by the judicial officers.
(ii) As regards uniformity of pay scales all over India the proposed legislation will serve
the purpose in respect of UTs for which the Central Government is administratively
responsible, under Article 309 of the Constitution read with Entry 11A of Concurrent
List.
(iii) The legislative Entry relating to appointment of subordinate courts is traceable to
entry 41 of List II, State List read with Articles 229 (2), 233 and 234 of the
Constitution. Accordingly, it may not be constitutionally feasible for the Union
Government to bring legislation to effect uniform pay scales in terms of the
directions of the Supreme Court in its Judgment of 21st March, 2002. However, the
Union Parliament is competent to make such law for the Union Territories.
(iv) States are free to implement the recommendations of FNJPC. As States are also
parties to the All India Judges’ Association Case, they are free to file their own
affidavits independently. Even one of the recommendations of the FNJPC i.e. the
Union Government should bear fifty per cent of the expenditure on subordinate
judiciary in the States has been rejected by the Supreme Court eventually.
(v) In regard to the questioning of expertise of the Ministry of Law and Justice in
framing pay scales, the Department of Justice has clarified that the Bill has been
formulated on the basis of a Cabinet decision, with inputs from the Ministry of
Finance which is the repository, of knowledge in fiscal matters and inputs from the
Law Ministry which has expertise and possess requisite qualifications and
competence to draft legislative bills.
(vi) Pay Commissions’ reports are only recommendatory in nature. The Government
reserves the right of accepting or rejecting such recommendation(s) either fully or
partially.
5.5 The Committee having noted the submissions of All India Judges Association and
responses of Department of Justice thereon, is of the considered view that the Cabinet is
the appropriate authority to take an overall view on the recommendations of the FNJPC.
Thereafter the Parliament/State Legislatures are the competent bodies to legislate in the
matter.
5.6 The Committee wishes to affirm that in terms of Articles 125, 221 and 309 (read with
Entry 11A of Concurrent List) of the Constitution, Parliament is supreme to make laws in
regard to the salaries and conditions of service of Judges of the Supreme Court, High

5
Courts and Sub-ordinate Judiciary of UTs. Under the Constitution, Parliament enjoys
exclusive powers in financial matters and no money could be spent from and out of the
Consolidated Fund of India, without its authorisation.
5.7 The Committee endorses the legislative route, which has been adopted by the Union
Government to vindicate the principle of parliamentary supremacy in authorisation of
expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India for the services of the Union.
6.0 The following paragraphs contain the observations/recommendations of the Committee with
regard to the clauses of the Bill.
Clause 2
6.1.0 Clause 2 provides for the definition of Judicial Officers, Schedule and Union Territories
used in the Bill.
6.1.1 The Clause is adopted without any change.
Clause 3
6.2.0 Clause 3 provides for the Salaries and Special Judicial Allowance (SJA) for the Judicial
Officers in the Union Territories. The details of pay scales are given in the Schedule to the Bill.
6.2.1 An amendment (Annexure IX) was moved to the proviso to sub-clause (2) for lowering
SJA to the extent that the SJA together with basic pay shall not exceed Rs.400/ - per mensem of
the highest scale of that post.
6.2.2 The Government’s view was that the proposed amendment might lead to a situation where
a person reaching the maximum of the pay scale in a particular grade may draw less than which
he was drawing before.
6.2.3 The Committee agrees with the explanation of the Government. The clause is
adopted without any change.
Clause 4
6.3.0 Clause 4 provides that subject to the provisions of clause 3, the rules and orders applicable
to judicial officers, immediately before the commencement of this legislation, shall continue to
regulate the condition of service of the judicial officers (other than SJA) unless otherwise provided
by rules made under this law.
6.3.1 An amendment (Annexure-IX) was moved for deleting the bracketed words “other than
special judicial allowance” appearing in the clause.
6.3.2 The Government accepted the amendment with modifications proposed in the marginal
heading as follows
“Rules and orders relating to conditions of service of judicial officers to continue to apply”.
6.3.3 The clause is adopted subject to the marginal heading being suitably modified.
Clause 5
6.4.0 Clause 5 provides for empowering the Union Government to make rules and orders
regulating the conditions of service and allowances (other than SJA), leave and pension of the
Judicial Officers in the UTs.

6
6.4.1 Clause is adopted without any change.
The Schedule
[See clauses 2(b) and 3 (1) of the Bill]
6.5.0 The Schedule provides for revised pay scales of judicial officers.
6.5.1 An amendment was moved in the Schedule that the scales at serials 2 and 3 be clubbed
together and it should be a running scale for Civil Judge and Senior Civil Judges and that there
should be no separate pay scale for Senior Civil Judge. The running scale should be Rs.10650-
16500/-
6.5.2 The Department has opined that clubbing the pay scales of Civil Judge (STS) and Senior
Civil Judge will disturb the existing hierarchy, as Senior Civil Judge is the promotion post of Civil
Judge (STS). Clubbing of these two pay scales will not only curtail the promotion avenues for Civil
Judges (STS) but also diminish the status of Senior Civil Judges, who are senior most judges in
the Lower Judicial Service. The Department has stated that the proposed amendment may not be
accepted.
6.5.3 The Committee notes the reply of the Government and agrees to the reasons
adduced.
6.5.4 The schedule is adopted without any change.
Financial Memorandum
6.6.0 Financial Memorandum appended to the Bill states that the recurring expenditure of about
Rs.76.56 lakhs per annum and non-recurring expenditure of Rs.5.16 crores towards payment of
arrears from the First day of July, 1996 would be charged from the Consolidated Fund of India.
6.6.1 It has been pointed out  to the Committee that under the scheme of the Constitution
such type of expenditure, except in respect of Supreme Court, should not be put under the
category ‘charged’ and instead should be under the category ‘voted’.
6.6.2 The Department of Justice conceded to the point raised and submitted that necessary
amendment in the Financial Memorandum would be carried out.
6.6.3 The Committee recommends that the Government may carry out  necessary
amendment in the Financial Memorandum to rectify the mistake.
Clause 1, Enacting Formula and the Title
6.7 Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title are adopted without any change.
7. The Committee recommends that the Bill as amended may be passed.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
It is expedient, in the public interest, to pass this legislation in respect of
members of the District and Subordinate Judiciary in the Union territories in
order—
(a) to set the salary of the Judicial Officers at a level which would
attract proper talent to opt for a career in judicial service;
(b) to provide pay scales and other conditions of service to the
members of Subordinate Judiciary which would satisfy their needs to
maintain a dignified way of life commensurate with the onerous duties that
they discharge and to boost their morale and commitment to service;
(c) to evolve distinct service conditions to the members of Subordinate
Judiciary in the Union territories keeping in view the prevailing relativities,
the judgments of various courts including the Supreme Court and the
financial position of the Government;
(d) to introduce a Special Judicial Allowance (SJA) as compensation
for their duties which involve essential work comprising of reading,
referencing, dictating judgments and preparing for cases beyond normal
working hours of courts.
2. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

Sir,
The All India Judges Association, which represents the “judicial services”  constituted
under Art. 233 and Art. 234 of the Constitution of India, all over the country, has come to know
that the Government of India, on 9th of May, 2003, has introduced in Lok Sabha, ‘The Salaries
and Allowances of the Judicial Officers of the Union Territories Bill, 2003’.  The said Bill, has
been referred to the Parliamentary Committee under your Chairmanship for consideration.
The Supreme Court in the All India Judges’ Association case (AIR 2993 SC 2493) directed
constitution of a separate Pay Commission for prescribing uniform pay scales including allowances
to the judges all over the country. The Court observed that judiciary is above the administrative
executive and any attempt to place it on par with the administrative executive has to be
discouraged.... and the service conditions of the judges which are wrongly linked to those of the
administrative executive have to be revised to meet the special needs of the judicial service. The
judgment became final and binding after all Review petitions by the Union of India and States, were
dismissed on 24th August, 1993, vide judgment reported as AIR 1993 SC 2493.
Pursuant to the directions and observations of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, the
Government of India by its Resolution dated the 21st March, 1996 (enclosed), notified constitution
of the First National Judicial Pay Commission for the Subordinate Judiciary of all the States and
Union Territories, amongst others, with the following terms of reference:
(a) To evolve the principles which should govern the structure of pay and other
emoluments of judicial officers belonging to the Subordinate Judiciary all over the
country.

40
(b) To examine the present structure of emoluments and conditions of service of taking
into account the total packet of benefits available to them and make suitable
recommendations having regard, among other relevant factors, to the existing
relativities in the pay structure between the officers belonging to Subordinate Judicial
Services vis-a-vis other Civil Servants.
(Clauses c and d not reproduced)
The First National Judicial Pay Commission, submitted its Report in 1999 to the Prime
Minister of India, Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee, and to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of India
for necessary acceptance. The Supreme Court in its different hearings heard the Union of India
and all the States through their Advocate Generals, and by its detailed judgment pronounced on
21st March, 2002, accepted the Report, subject to modifications of some recommendations. The
court allowed time till 1st July, 2002. The Court from time to time further extended time to Union
of India and the States, on their requests to make budgetary allocations. The Court admitted for
consideration some points raised by the Union of India, in relations to some allowances, which are
still sub-judice. The Union of India did not file any application on the payment of pay scales, but
only sought more time for finances as was also the case with some States. On the last monitoring
hearing on implementation of the order, all States made statement that they will pass/have passed
orders implementing the judgment on judicial commission recommendations. The Union of India, on
behalf of various Union Territories, through the Attorney General, made submissions that showed
that it was so seeking time not for implementing the recommendations but to move a legislation
to nullify the final and binding order, by not agreeing with the Court Order. The Attorney General
indicated the introduction of Bill at a time when Court was seeking
The Association submits that the proclamation of public interest  mentioned in the Statement
of Objects and Reasons in the Bill, is directly opposed to the recommendations of the Judicial Pay
Commission, which was constituted by the Government of India itself by its Resolution of
21st March, 1996, with specific terms of reference. The Bill has recommended scales of pay and
allowances, which are totally on a different pattern than those recommended by the Commission
and accepted by the Supreme Court. The Bill seeks to introduce the scales of pay which are even
lower than the existing scales of pay in different Union Territories, and are also opposed to the
new scales of pay recommended by Judicial Commission and directed  by the Supreme Court. The
lower scales of pay, far from attracting proper talent to a career in judicial service, will not only
dissuade new comers, but will also demoralize the existing incumbents. This is also incomplete
inasmuch as it does not deal with all the allowances listed in the judgment of apex court accepting
the recommendations.
The Association submits that the Special Judicial Allowance provided in the Bill, in place of
replacing the old scales with new ones is nothing but an attempt to place the judiciary at par or
below administrative executive, rather than to discourage it as directed by the Supreme Court
leading to, setting up of separate Pay Commission.
The Association submits that the Government has not only attempted to mislead the
Committee of the Parliament but also the Parliament itself, by not suppressing in the Bill, the fact
of Government of India Resolution of 21st March, 1996, constituting the First National Judicial Pay
Commission, the fact of its submitting its Report after hearing all Governments and Union
Territories and High Court, the fact of Supreme Court accepting the recommendations and directing
its implementation in its final judgment dated 21st March, 2002, and continuing monitoring by the
Apex Court.
The Bill moved by the Government shows no reasons, to differ with the recommendations
of the First National Judicial Pay Commission, in case of judges of Union Territories, especially when
the Supreme Court has directed the implementation of the recommendations uniformly all over India.

41
The Association submits that number of States have already implemented the pay scales as
approved by the Supreme Court. The Bill, which seeks to recommend different and lower scales
of pay than those implemented for other judicial officers in other States, would be in direct conflict
with the original judgment of Apex Court which directed separate Pay Commission to achieve the
uniformity in scales of pay and allowances all over the country.
The Association is of the view that such a confrontational approach of the Government of
India, is not only subversive of the Rule of Law in a democracy, but also extremely contemptuous
of the highest court of the land, besides abuse of legislative power in a reprehensible manner.

Our further submission is that the subject matter of the proposed bill can not be raised

Strangely the Union Government seeks to secure surruptuously the suppression of the

Members of the Parliament in complete dark by suppressing the material facts and events
about the pendency of the All India Judges Association case and also about the existence
of the said three judgements/orders of the Supreme Court, to which case the Union
Government and all States including Union Territories, are parties. The Association is of the

action, the initiation of the proposed Bill has been undertaken.
2. We respectfully point out that the opening words in the statement of objects and reasons
viz. : “it is expedient, in the public interest, to pass this legislation in respect of members
of the District and  Subordinate Judiciary in the Union Territories”  are disingenuous.
Public interest would not be served by passing this Bill simply because it will put in reverse
gear all that has been attempted or done in this past seven years:
(a) The question with regard to pay scales in respect of members of the judicial service
was first referred to the 5th Pay Commission, but by  an amendment made on
24.10.1996, the reference to 5th Pay Commission with regard to the Pay Scales of
Judicial Officers was deleted. This was because of the appointment of First National
Judicial Pay Commission known as Justice Shetty Commission by a Government
Resolution of 21st March, 1996.

(c) As the Vth Central Pay Commission Report had been accepted but no relief was
available to the members of the Judicial Subordinate Service, a question arose that
pending the recommendation of the Shetty Commission whether any interim orders can
be passed giving some relief. Accordingly, on 16th December, 1997, another term of

3. Further, the All India Judges Association is of the form of view that the Union Government
has no right to introduce legislation to set at nought the legal effect of the three judgements/
orders already passed by the Supreme Court to which they are party and try to circumvent
them by introducing the proposed legislation.
It is settled Law that a binding judicial pronouncement between parties cannot be made
ineffective with the aid of any legislative power by enacting a provision which in substance
overrules such judgment and is not realm of legislative enactment which displaces the basis
of foundation of the judgment and uniformly applies to a class of persons concerned with
the entire subject sought to be covered by such an enactment having retrospective effect.
The legislature can change the basis on which a decision is given by the Court and thus,
change the law in general which will affect a class of persons and event at large. It cannot,
however, set aside a decision inter party. Such an act on the part of the legislature amounts
to exercising the judicial power of the State and to functioning as an Appellate Court or
Tribunal, S.R. Bhagwat v. State of Mysore, (1995) 6 SCC 16: AIR 1996 SC 188.
The legislature under our Constitution have within the prescribed limit, power to make laws
prospectively as well as retrospectively. By exercise of those powers, the legislature can
remove the basis of a decision rendered by a competent Court thereby rendering that
decision ineffective. But the legislature has no jurisdiction within the certain limits to amend
the provision to the Act retrospectively and to declare what a law shall be deemed to have
been, but it is not open to the legislature to say that the judgement of the Court properly
constituted and rendered in exercise of this power in a matter brought before it shall be
deemed to be ineffective and the interpretation of the law shall be otherwise than as
declared by the Constitution, (1) State of Tamil Nadu v.  M Rayappa, AIR 1971 SC 231
(1971) 3 SSC 1, (2) Municipal Corporation of the City of Ahmadabad v. New Shrock Spg

Central Provinces Ltd. v.  Amalgamated Coal Field Ltd., AIR 1971 SC 57 : (1970) 1 SCC
509.

In the light of all the above, a most serious question arises for consideration under your
distinguished Chairmanship, Sir, as to whether, and if so, what report at all should be
submitted by the Hon’ble Committee to the Parliament.

The All India Judges Association would like the Hon’ble Committee to formulate the
following issue or question for consideration in the light of various submissions made by the

Whether the Bill under consideration does not seek to dismiss three final and binding
judgments of Hon’ble Supreme Court namely main judgment in the case of All India Judges
Association vs. Union of India and others reported as AIR 1992 SC 165; the Review
Judgment reported as AIR 1993 SC 2493 and the latest judgment of 21st March, 2002,

First National Judicial Pay Commission, in so far as it related to the judicial officers of the
Union Territories?
The Association makes following submissions in respect of the Bill in the light of various
facts and circumstances as mentioned hereunder:
The Clause 1(3) of the Bill states that the Bill shall be deemed to have come into force on
the 1st day of July,  1996. The First National Judicial Commission recommendations are to
be effective with effect from the same date as also directed by the Supreme Court
Judgment of 21st March, 2003. The Association submits that the effect of this clause
would be to efface and superceding the directions of the Supreme Court giving effect to

request the Committee to seek clarifications on this aspect from the Union Government.
2. The scales of pay mentioned in the Schedule to the Bill shows that the scales of pay

9th May, 2003, that the pay scales as recommended by the Shetty Commission should be
implemented in the letter and spirit and uniformly.
3. The Union of India has yet to file an affidavit indicating the date from which the
recommendations in terms of the orders of the Court will be implemented, though, the time
of 10 weeks sought by the Attorney General has elapsed. The Association would request
the Committee to seek clarifications from the Government on this aspect.
4. In the face of final and binding judgment of Supreme Court in the Main case AIR 1992
SC 165 ordering uniformity in the scales of pay of all the judicial officers, throughout India
and the constitution of First National Judicial Pay Commission with the a term of reference
on this aspect of uniformity, the BILL does not show any reason or intelligible differentia
to have a separate treatment for the judicial officers of the Union Territories. The
Association would request the Committee to advice the Government on the binding nature
of the Supreme Court judgment. The Supreme Court in its latest order held that there
should be some specific and valid reason if departure was to be made from the
recommendations of the Pay Commissions.

47

and Reasons melt away if one reads the affidavit of Shri Tabom Barn, Joint Secretary in

that under the modifications the officers will get much more than what they get under the
Shetty Commission. The Association requests the Committee to get the matter enquired into
by ordering the records of the Government to know the reason. The apparent reason spelled
out by the Attorney General in open court was that it was a class war referring to IAS
and other services and the feeling of jealousy, for which the Government was doing some
balancing. The said reason only ridicules and hits at the law of the land that there can be

Sir,
Under your most distinguished Chairmanship, the Association on 3rd September, 2003, had
the privilege of presenting its views, evidence and submissions on the Bill on the Salaries and
Allowances of the Judicial of the Union Territories, which is presently with the Committee under
your Chairmanship. We are grateful to provide us an additional opportunity to furnish factual data
with regard to pay scales approved by the Hon’ble Supreme Court vis-a-vis  the pay scales
proposed in the Bill, for the purpose of highlighting the disparities for consideration of the
Committee.
We are to submit that with regard to pay scales, the Shetty Commission set out the
principles governing the pay structure of the subordinate Judiciary. It referred to All India Judges’
Association case wherein it had been observed that the parity in status should be between the
political executive, the legislature and the Judges and not between the Judges and the administrative
executive.
After taking into consideration the recommendations which had been made by the Fifth
Central Pay Commission, and getting an independent study and report from the Indian Institute of
Public Administration, New Delhi, and the pivotal role of the subordinate Judiciary and the essential
characteristics of a judicial officer, the Shetty Commission evolved a master pay scale of
Rs.9000-24,850.  It concluded that the number of pay scales should be equal to the number of
clearly identifiable levels of responsibility and extremely narrow scope of promotional avenues in
judicial services.

In the table above, words ACP scale stand for Assured Career Progression scale.
The table also indicates that in judicial service there are only two  clearly identifiable level
of responsibility corresponding to two entry-level scales at (i) and (v) above. These two levels
respectively, are in terms of Recruitment under Article 234 Article 233 of the Constitution of India
in the Chapter VI of the Part VI of the Constitution. These services in the language of Constitution
of India are described as SUBORDINATE COURTS. Though, by long usage the judges presiding
over in these courts have come to be described as Judicial Officers.
The Commission provided the ACP scales only in the “judicial service” below District Judge
level. This is to avoiding long and peculiar stagnation in the very nature of judicial service, in which
there is only one promotional level of appellate court of District Judges.
The Commission in its Report stated that it was only trying to set the salary at a level that
allows aspirants with modest backgrounds, and with family responsibilities, to accept the challenge
of judicial service and a level that does not progressively penalize those dedicated individuals who
choose to serve and make sacrifices in terms of loneliness and general withdrawal from community
affairs serve the public.
In arriving at the previously mentioned pay scales DESCRIBED IN THE TABLE ABOVE,
the Commission noted that while fixing the maximum of the master pay scale it had been
constrained by the vertical cap of the salaries of the High Court Judges. In other words, the
District Judges could not get more salary than a High Court Judge whose salary was statutorily
fixed. It, however, recommended that as and when the salary of a High Court Judge is raised, and
then the salary of the judicial officers should be increase by maintaining the ratio that it had
recommended. According to the Commission, the pay scales recommended by it should be deemed
to come into force with effect from 1.7.96.
The Union of India was heard at length through its Solicitor General on the above scales
of pay before the same were accepted and directed to be implemented w.e.f. 1.1.96 by its judgment
dated 21st March, 2002.
The Association submits that the total expenditure involved in respect of revision of pay
scales of UT officers does not exceed Rs.2.50 crores. This is based on information supplied to
the Supreme Court in the affidavit of Shri D.C. Gupta, Secretary (Expenditure).

NOTE/REMARKS:
The Association submits that the Judicial Officers cannot be compared in any manner
and for any purpose with the officers in the executive branch of the Government. The Judicial
Officers can be compared only with their nearest equals in functioning. The nearest equals in
terms of nature of duties of judicial officers are in their own judicial family consisting of High
Court Judges or Supreme Court Judges. Their scales of pay and other service conditions are to
be related to the salaries and conditions of superior judiciary. It is respectfully submitted that
the range of scales of salaries starting from Rs.8000/- going up to Rs.26,000 are to be shared
on equal footing by the Judicial wing of the State. In prescribing or assignment of scales within
judiciary, by the Supreme Court, on the basis of recommendations of a duly constituted Pay
Commission, the executive wing of Government should not complain as, parity in range of
scales of pay is duly maintained and not at all disturbed with the highest salary of High Court
judges statutorily fixed at Rs.26,000/-.
The Association submits that only the Tribunals constituted by Government under Article
312 or other statutes can be considered to be somewhat nearly equals in Government. The
monetary compensation which the Government pays for performing the quasi-judicial function
in Tribunals, when it appoints its own officers in these tribunals for the judicial function,
provides another test to know the salaries for the judicial officers performing pure judicial
functions in Courts. The Government appoints DISTRICT JUDGES and other
ADMINISTRATIVE MEMBERS in these tribunals on the scale of pay of Rs.18,400-22,400. In the
face of this position, the Government cannot prescribe scale of Rs.15,100/- to Rs.18,300/- for
entry level District Judges, of similar rank as in Tribunals, when they are working in Judiciary
proper.

14. The Association invites your attention to the following observations of the Supreme Court,
which have a direct bearing on the Bill and whole matter:
“The most important point in these proceedings appears to us to be as to whether
the recommendations of the Shetty Commission laying down different scales of pay should
be accepted or not. It is to be borne in mind that pursuant to the judgment in the review
case (All India Judges Case) the Central Government had accepted the recommendations
and had  constituted the Shetty Commission. Correspondingly, it had  deleted from the terms
of reference of the Fifth Central Pay Commission the consideration in respect of the pay
scales  of  judicial officers. Therefore, it can safely be concluded that the  Central
Government had agreed to set up a Pay Commission  specifically for  judicial officers and
normally the  recommendations made in that behalf should be accepted unless  for some
specific and valid reason a departure was required to  be made...It was, therefore,. rightly
urged by Shri F.S. Nariman  that there must be good and compelling reasons for the States
and the Central Government in  not accepting the Shetty Commission.”

54
FUNDAMENTAL ERROR
The Association further draws your attention to a fundamental error committed by
the Union of India, in recommending its own scales to members of judicial service,
formulated on the basis that there should be a parity between the executive and judiciary.,
even though this was contrary to the decision of the Court in All India Judges’ Association.
Case as well as in the review judgment, where it was stated in no uncertain terms that
the judiciary could not be equated with the executive and it must have its own pay
structure.
The Court in Para 17 of the judgment already enclosed with the submissions
observed as under on the aspect of mistake even based on parity.
“Even if we were to examine the two scales of pay, one for the IAS officers after
the Fifth Central Pay Commission Report and he scales of pay recommended for the
judicial service, we find that there is a fundamental error which has been committed
by the Union of India. The scales of pay approved for the IAS officers are as follows:
Junior scale Rs.8000-13,500
Senior scale:
(i) Time scale Rs.10,650-15,850
(ii) Jr . Admn. grade Rs.12,750-16,500
(iii) Selection grade Rs.15,100-18,300
(iv) Super time scale Rs.18,400-22,400
(v) Above ST scale Rs.22,400-24,500
Secretary To Government of India Rs.26,000/-(fixed)
Cabinet Secretary Rs.30,000/-(fixed)
“18. What the Union of India has done is that it equated the District Judge at the
entry level with the selection grade for the IAS officers. The pay scale approved is
Rs.15,100-18,300. We, however, find that an IAS officer enters the selection grade
after having put in approximately 14 years of service. On the other hand, a Civil
Judge, would normally enter the level of the District Judge, and is appointed first as
an Additional District Judge, are having put in 18 to 20 years of services far as the
IAS officers are concerned, cafter 17 years of service, an IAS officer would normal
enter the super time scale of 18,400-22,400. If the number of years which are put
in service, is a measure to be adopted in determining as what should be the pay
scales, we find that the Government of India has erred in equating the District Judge
at the entry level with the scale of pay of a selection grade IAS officer; The proper
equation should have been between the District Judge at the entry level with a super
time scale of an IAS officer. It is on that basis that the scales of pay should have
been determined.”
“19...The scale of pay of Rs.16,750-20,500 recommended by the Shetty Commission
is lower than the super time scale. for an IAS officer of Rs.18,400-22,400, when such
an officer enters the super tike scale after 17 years of service. A judicial officer
enters the selection grade of a District Judge after having put in 21 to 25 years of
service. The pay scale recommended by the Shetty Commission Rs.18,750-22850. This
is less than the scale above ST scale recommended for an IAS officer which is of
Rs.22,400-24,500 even though as IAS officer enters that scale after having put in
25 years of service which is on a par with the number of years put in by a judicial

55
officer on his entry into selection grade. It is only the District Judge (super time
scale) as recommended by the Shetty Commission which is comparable with the last
scale of an IAS officer.”
Concluding on the aspect of pay scales the court continued as under:
“20. From the aforesaid, it is clear, and it is so mentioned in the Shetty
Commission Report, that the said Commission has  taken into consideration the
recommendations of the Fifth  Central Pay Commission while determining the pay
scales for  the judicial officers. In our opinion, the pay Scales recommended by the
Shetty Commission are just and reasonable. Considering, the years of service put in
by the judicial officers at different stages, the parity in the scales of pay
recommended by the Shetty Commission for the judicial officers with the scales of
pay of IAS officers is not, by and large  disturbed. In fact, the scales of pay
recommended by the Shetty  Commission appears to us to be somewhat lower, on the
average  than the scales of pay recommended for an IAS officer if we  take into
consideration, as we must do, the number of years a judicial officer has put in
service. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the pay scales recommended by the
Shetty Commission should be accepted. We wish to emphasize that even though in
the earlier judgments, it has rightly been said that there should be no equation or
parity between judicial service and the executive service,  
nevertheless even on the
basis that there should not be great  distortion in the pay scales of the judicial
offices vis-a-vis executive, we find the recommendations made by Shetty Commission
are just, fair and reasonable.”
The above discussion. would show that the Bill only seeks to create
discrimination and disparity between equals in violation of Article 14 of the
Constitution of India, an article of faith. It can never be in public interest to provide
inequality between equals. The provisions in the Bill clearly show that the scales have
been arbitrarily framed by closing eyes to what is discussed in the binding judgment of
the Supreme Court on 21st  March, 2002. 
The Bill, if passed as it is, would defeat object
of having uniformity in service conditions of judges in the countr y.
The Association, therefore, prays that the Committee under your distinguished
and experienced Chairmanship makes a suitable comprehensive report to the
Parliament to consider removing an disparities in letter and spirit in the light of
various discriminations and difficulties brought to your notice by way of  our view,
evidence, submissions and what is mentioned above in this communication.
The Association would also request to the Hon’ble Committee of the
Parliament on Home Affairs to suggest to the Government to first correct the
fundamental error, as pointed out by the Supreme Court, in prescribing incorrect
scales of pay, and then only a comprehensive Bill should be considered, if required.
